O Indra, just as you drank the former Soma juices, drink also the juice now offered. May this juice satisfy you. Hear our praise. And grow by our praises. Make the sun manifest. Bring foods to us. Destroy our enemies. O Indra, cause the cows that were carried off to come back.
Drink it as of old, and may it exhilarate you : hear our prayer, and be exalted by our praises ; make the sum visible, nourish us with food, destory our enemies, rescue the cattle.

In this Ṛk also Indra is prayed to drink Soma. Just as in many earlier sacrifices Indra drank Soma and favoured the sacrificers, so now too he is prayed to drink Soma and release the cows carried off by the Paṇis. And it is also stated here that after Indra released the cows, he set the sun, which had been covered by darkness, in the atmosphere and made it shine.⟨NOTE:316⟩
notes: ದಾವನ್ / ಒದಗಿಸಲಿ "may provide" in the Kannada; Sāyaṇa glosses ಧಾವನ್ ಅಗಚ್ಛನ್ "ran, went": the vessels are filled with Soma

en: O Indra, possessed of food, these intoxicating Somas that have been drunk make you, the resplendent, exceedingly drenched; may they sprinkle you. And further, O Indra, may the intoxicating Somas greatly gladden you. What kind of you? Great and abundant; अनूनं (*anūnaṃ*), not deficient in any of the qualities, that is, of complete qualities; mighty, grown great; glorious, possessed of power; the overcomer of enemies.

O Indra, possessed of food, may these Soma juices, which are intoxicating and have been drunk, fill you, the resplendent, exceedingly. May these intoxicating Soma juices gladden you, who are great-souled, endowed with all qualities, grown great, possessed of power, assailant of enemies.

Abounding in food, Indra, let these exhilarating draughts copiously bedew you, the resplendent : let the inebriating juices delight you, who are mighty, deficient in no (excellence), powerful, manifold, the overcomer of foes.

O Indra, you were exhilarated by those Somas, and by them you settled Sūrya, the god who impels all, and Uṣas, the dawn goddess, each in its own place. Or else: you brought it about that Sūrya and Uṣas drive away the darknesses as they do. Doing what? Tearing apart the solid, that is, firm, darknesses. And further, O Indra, you thrust at the great mountain that lay all around the cows carried off by the Paṇis, a mountain unmoved from its own seat, that is, unshaken, indestructible, firm.
- आवासयः (*āvāsayaḥ*)—you established, each in its own place
- अप दर्द्रत् (*apa dardrat*)—you drove far away
- स्वात् सदसः परि (*svāt sadasaḥ pari*)—from its own place
- गाः परि (*gāḥ pari*)—all around the cows

O Indra, you who were satisfied by drinking those very Soma juices established the sun and the dawn each in its own place. You drove the dense darknesses far away. O Indra, you pierced and thrust into the mountain that stood unmoved from its own place, that surrounded and pervaded the cows, and that was vast.

By which (juices) being exhilarated you have appointed the sun and the dawn (to their offices), driving away the solid (glooms) : you have penetrated, Indra, the mountain, unmoved from its own seat, concealing the cattle.

As explained in the third Ṛk of this sūkta, in this Ṛk also it is stated that after Indra had released the cows that were in the mountain caves, he made Uṣas and Sūrya, who had been covered with darkness in the atmosphere, shine again.

O Indra, by your wisdom, by your deeds and by your power, in the unripe cows you have set the ripe, that is, matured, famed milk, and you hold it firmly. And further, O Indra, for the cows, in order to bring the cows out, you opened the firm doors, that is, the doors made firm by Vala with stones and the like.
Accompanied by the Aṅgirases, you drove out the cows from the herd, that is, from the cow-pen; you made them go out.
- नि दीधः (*ni dīdhaḥ*)—you caused them to hold
- वि और्णोः (*vi aurṇoḥ*)—you caused to be released and opened
- अंगिरस्वान् (*aṃgirasvān*)—you who were with the Aṅgirases

O Indra, by your wisdom, by your deeds and by your power, you caused the unripe cows to hold ripe and famed milk. You caused the exceedingly firm doors to be released and opened for the entry of those cows. You who were with the Aṅgirases released the cows from the cow-pen and made them come out.

By your wisdom, by your deeds, through your power, you have developed the mature (milk) in the immature (udders), you have opened the strong doors for the cattle (to come forth): associated with the Angirasas. you have liberated the cows from their fold.

The wisdom and the surpassing power of Indra are fathomless. Cows that until then had not given milk begin to give milk as soon as they have calved. To cause milk to be filled in such unripe cows is one of the heroic deeds of Indra. In order to release the cows that the Paṇis had shut up in the mountain caves, he removed the boulders that had been put across the doors of the cave and made the cows come out. This is Indra's second deed. That Indra did these two kinds of deeds is described here as showing the power, strength and qualities of Indra. The filling of the cows with milk, and also the matter of setting the sun in the atmosphere and making it shine, are
described in Ṛks such as आमासु पक्वमैय आ सूर्यं रोहयो दिवि (*āmāsu pakvamaiya ā sūryaṃ rohayo divi*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-89-7) **GLOSS**

O Indra, by your great deed you have filled, extended, the wide earth. O Indra, mighty one, you prop up the vast heaven: as heaven stands without support and yet does not fall, Indra so acts. And further, you sustain the two worlds, heaven and earth, by nourishments. Of what kind are they? They are those whose sons are the gods; ancient; parents, makers, of the ṛta, that is, of water or of sacrifice; mighty. Or else: they are the parents of the whole world, and the mighty children of ṛta, that is, of Brahman; yahu is a name for offspring.⟨NOTE:317⟩
notes: ಯದ್ವಾ ವಾತೇರ್ವಾತಂ । ಅನಭಿಗತಃ: the derivation is damaged or unclear

en: - उप स्तभायः (*upa stabhāyaḥ*)—you have held up
- देवपुत्रे (*devaputre*)—having the gods as their sons

O Indra, by your great deed you have pervaded the exceedingly wide earth. You, great-souled, have held up the exceedingly abundant world of heaven. You have held up heaven and earth, who have the gods as their sons, who are ancient, who are the makers of everything, and who are the mighty parents of the sacrifice.

You have filled the wide earth, Indra, with (the fame of) your deeds : you, the mighty one, have propped up the vast heaven: you have sustained the heaven and earth, whose children are the gods, (and who are) the old and mighty parents of sacrifice.

Now, at this time, all the gods, Agni and the others, O Indra, have put you in front for battle, you who are the chief, mighty and strong one; when the non-god Vṛtra, the Asura, advanced against the gods for battle (the root oh has the sense of going).

And further, at this time, in the battle, the Maruts resort to Indra (the subject, the Maruts, is to be supplied): the meaning is that when the gods had fled, the Maruts resorted to Indra. The connection is that now they put him in front.
- पुरः दधिरे (*puraḥ dadhire*)—placed in front of themselves
- अत्र स्वर्षाता (*atra svarṣātā*)—in such a battle
O Indra, when Vṛtra opposed the gods, at that time all the gods placed you, the chief and the mighty, in front of themselves for battle. In such battles the Maruts remain with Indra and serve him.
All the gods then placed you, Indra, as their mighty chief in front for battle: when the impious (Asuras) assailed the deities: the Maruts supported Indra in the conflict.

In the four or five Ṛks that follow, it is described that Indra destroyed the Asura Vṛtra. The matter is also mentioned that at the time of the slaying of Vṛtra the Marut deities were with Indra and helped Indra.

The famous heaven, the support of the gods, O Indra, now, at this time, bowed away out of a twofold fear: fear of your thunderbolt and fear of your own wrath. The particle "nu" is only a filler. When Indra, who has abundant food, slew Vṛtra the serpent, who came against him, so that he should lie down, that is, for his death, at that time the heaven bowed away. The particle "cit" is likewise a filler. The connection is: when he slew Vṛtra, at that time the heaven bowed.
- द्विता (*dvitā*)—by a twofold power, that is
- अप अनमत् (*apa anamat*)—bowed down in humility

O Indra, you who have abundant food and are the lord: when you slew Vṛtra, who opposed you, so that he was destroyed, at that time the famous heaven too bowed down in humility, from the fear produced by your twofold power, that is, by your thunderbolt and by your wrath.
The heaven bowed down in the two-fold dread of your thunderbolt, and your individual wrath, when Indra, the giver of food, struck to the sleep (of death) the assailing Ahi.

Now, O fierce Indra, whose strength is exalted, Tvaṣṭṛ, the craftsman of the gods, fashioned for you, the mighty one, the thunderbolt, that is, brought it to completion. It has a thousand streams and a hundred edges. O Indra, possessor of the Soma whose juice is spent, you crushed with that thunderbolt the serpent Vṛtra, the Asura, who makes a noise. He is described as one whose desire is fixed, and as one whose mind goes swiftly against his enemies. The meaning is that you made that thunderbolt and crushed him.
- ऋजीशिन् (*ṛjīśin*)—you who possess the Soma juice that is spent
- आरमणसं (*āramaṇasaṃ*)—him who has a tendency to rush against
- त्वष्टा (*tvaṣṭā*)—Tvaṣṭṛ, the craftsman of the gods

O Indra, you who possess the Soma whose juice is spent, and who are of terrible form: the thunderbolt with which you struck and pulverised, until you were satisfied, Vṛtra, who has a tendency to rush against you and who makes noise, that thunderbolt with its thousand streams and its hundred joints Tvaṣṭṛ, the craftsman of the gods, made and gave in good time to you, who are of mighty form.
Fierce Indra, Twashtri constructed for you, the mighty one, the thousand-edged, the hundred-angled thunderbolt, wherewith you have crushed the ambitious, audacious, loud-shouting Ahi.

सहस्रभृष्टिं शताश्रिं वज्रं महः ते त्वष्टा अध ववृतत् (*sahasrabhṛṣṭiṃ śatāśriṃ vajraṃ mahaḥ te tvaṣṭā adha vavṛtat*)—this Ṛk describes the thunderbolt. This thunderbolt has thousands of blades and hundreds of sharp points. It is said here that Tvaṣṭṛ, the craftsman of the gods, made such a thunderbolt for Indra.
अहन्न हिं पर्वते शिश्रियाणं त्वष्टास्मै वज्रं स्वर्यं ततक्ष । (*ahanna hiṃ parvate śiśriyāṇaṃ tvaṣṭāsmai vajraṃ svaryaṃ tatakṣa |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-32-2)
मह्यं त्वष्टा वज्रमतक्षदायसं मयि देवासोवृजन्नपि क्रतुं । (*mahyaṃ tvaṣṭā vajramatakṣadāyasaṃ mayi devāsovṛjannapi kratuṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-48-3)
In these and other Ṛks there is the description of Tvaṣṭṛ making the thunderbolt of iron for Indra.
O Indra, all the Maruts, delighted together, all the gods, exalt you with hymns. For you, the god named Pūṣan and the god named Viṣṇu...

...cook a hundred buffaloes, that is, a hundred male animals; may they cook them. And for you the three vessels called Droṇakalaśa, Pūtabhṛt and Ādhavanīya go to the Soma, the Soma runs to them; the meaning is that the vessels are filled with Soma. Of what kind is the Soma? Inebriating, and slaying Vṛtras, that is, enemies. Here "Vṛtra-slaying" is said of Soma, for when Soma has been drunk Indra becomes able to slay Vṛtras.
- वर्धान् (*vardhān*)—who praised and made you grow strong
- त्रीणि सरांसि (*trīṇi sarāṃsi*)—also the three vessels called Droṇakalaśa, Pūtabhṛt and Ādhavanīya

O Indra, all the Maruts, having the same affection, praised you and made you grow strong. For such a you, may the god Pūṣan and Viṣṇu cook a hundred male animals. May the three vessels, Droṇakalaśa, Pūtabhṛt and Ādhavanīya, also provide for you the inebriating Soma that destroys Vṛtra.⟨NOTE:318⟩
notes: ಮೃಕ್ಷತಿಃ ಸಂಸ್ಥೇಹನಕರ್ಮಾ ... ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಹನಕರ್ತಾ: the printed readings of "saṃsthehana" differ and are unclear

en: For you, Indra, whom all the Maruts, alike pleased, exalt, may Pushan and Vishnu dress for you a hundred buffaloes, and to him may the three streams flow with the inebriating, foe-destroying Soma.

पूषा विष्णुः शतं महिषान् पचत् (*pūṣā viṣṇuḥ śataṃ mahiṣān pacat*)—it is prayed here that the god named Pūṣan and Viṣṇu may cook for you, O Indra, a hundred animals (buffaloes). The matter of Indra eating the flesh of these animals is stated in many places, but each place has a different number. For example:
पचंति ते वृषभा अत्सि तेषां पृक्षेण यन्मघवन् हूयमानः । (*pacaṃti te vṛṣabhā atsi teṣāṃ pṛkṣeṇa yanmaghavan hūyamānaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-28-3)
O Indra, the sacrificing yajamānas cook for you bulls or oxen, that is, the flesh of oxen. It is said in this Ṛk that you eat it. Here there is no statement of the number of oxen.
अमा ते तुम्रं वृषभं पचानि तीव्रं सुतं पंचदशं नि षिंचं । (*amā te tumraṃ vṛṣabhaṃ pacāni tīvraṃ sutaṃ paṃcadaśaṃ ni ṣiṃcaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-27-2)
The seer says that he will cook one ox (its flesh) for Indra and will prepare and offer Soma juice in fifteen vessels.
घसत्त इंद्र उक्षणः प्रियं काचित्करं हविर्विश्वस्मादिंद्र उत्तरः । (*ghasatta iṃdra ukṣaṇaḥ priyaṃ kācitkaraṃ havirviśvasmādiṃdra uttaraḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-86-2)
May Indra eat the flesh of the ox. May he eat the pleasing oblation.
उक्ष्णो हि मे पंचदश साकं पचंति विंशतिं । (*ukṣṇo hi me paṃcadaśa sākaṃ pacaṃti viṃśatiṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-86-14)
Indra has said that the yajamānas cook for him fifteen and twenty bulls (oxen).
शतं महिषान् क्षीरपाकमोदनं वराहमिंद्र एमुषं । (*śataṃ mahiṣān kṣīrapākamodanaṃ varāhamiṃdra emuṣaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-77-10)
Here the matter of cooking a hundred buffaloes is stated, and
सखा सख्ये अपचित्तूयमग्निरस्य क्रत्वा महिषा त्रि शतानि । (*sakhā sakhye apacittūyamagnirasya kratvā mahiṣā tri śatāni |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-29-7)
here there is also mention of the cooking of the flesh of three hundred buffaloes.

O Indra, you let flow the water of the rivers, the streams, which was great, covered, enveloped and standing all around by Vṛtra; the meaning is that by this the rivers flowed full. You let loose the wave, the mass, of the waters; the repetition is for emphasis. O Indra, you made the paths of those rivers run along the slopes; "anu" is a preposition whose verb has to be supplied. Further, you drove the waters, which turned downwards towards the slope, that is, were full of speed, to the ocean, the sea. "Apasaḥ" has here the sense of "waters". Here the verb "ard" has the sense of leading.
- नदीनां क्षोदः (*nadīnāṃ kṣodaḥ*)—the water of the rivers
- आ अस्पृजः (*ā aspṛjaḥ*)—you released and made flow
- प्रवतः पंथां (*pravataḥ paṃthāṃ*)—having paths of flow

O Indra, you released and made flow the water of the rivers, which was great, held back by Vṛtra and standing all around. O Indra, you also made paths for those same floods. You made the waters that flow into the low regions flow to the ocean.

You have set free the greatly obstructed and arrested water of the rivers, the afflux of the waters : you have directed them, Indra, upon their downward paths : you have sent them rapidly down to the ocean.

O Indra, may our new prayer, a hymn made by us and never made before by others, turn you towards our protection, that is, bring you to us for our protection. What kind of Indra? One who, in the manner stated, has done all those famous deeds; the lord; great, mighty; fierce, that is, full of vigour; unaging; the giver of might, that is, of strength; one whose Maruts are excellent heroes; well-armed, that is, having excellent weapons; and furnished with an excellent thunderbolt.

O Indra, you who, as described above, have accomplished all deeds, who are the lord, great-souled, full of vigour, free from decay, the giver of strength, accompanied by heroic Maruts, possessed of excellent weapons and distinguished by the thunderbolt: may our new hymn bring you to us for our protection.

May our new prayer bring to our protection you, Indra, who are the maker of all these (things that exist) : who are mighty, fierce, undecaying the giver of strength, having excellent descendants, the Maruts, well-armed, the bearer of the thunderbolt.

O Indra, you, such as you are, uphold us, who are radiant and wise, for strength, for fame, for food and for wealth; that is, sustain us. Further, O Indra, in me, Bharadvāja, make those who have men, that is, attendants, your praisers, my sons and grandsons; the verb is to be supplied. O Indra, be our protector on the coming day, the day to be crossed; the meaning is, be indeed our guardian.
- राये च (*rāye ca*)—and also for wealth
- सूरीन् (*sūrīn*)—sons and others who praise you (grant)
- पारै च दिवि (*pārai ca divi*)—on the coming days also

O Indra, you, the famous, who are radiant and wise: nourish us by giving us food, fame, strength and wealth. Grant to me, Bharadvāja, sons and others who have attendants and who praise you. O Indra, be our protector on the coming days also.

Resplendent Indra, uphold us who are devout, for (the obtaining of) food, of sustenancec, of nourishment, of wealth : bestow upon Bharadwaja pious posterity, with numerous attendants : be with us, Indra, every future day.
In this Ṛk, which is the conclusion of this sūkta, and in the next Ṛk, the seer Bharadvāja prays to Indra to give him wealth and the like, food, heroic sons and a long life.

On the sixth day, at the third pressing, in the śastra of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the third verse of the anurūpa triplet is "ayā vājam". It is also set out in the sūtra: अया वाजं देवहितं सनेमेति स्तोत्रियानुरूप् (*ayā vājaṃ devahitaṃ sanemeti stotriyānurūp*) (Ā. 8-3). By this praise may we share the food given by Indra, the shining god, who is the benefactor of the gods. And, blessed with excellent sons, may we rejoice for a hundred years.
- अया (*ayā*)—as the result of this praise
May we enjoy the food given by Indra as the result of this praise. Together with excellent sons, may we live happily for a hundred years.
May we, by this (praise), obtain food granted by the deity : may we. blessed with excellent male descendants, be happy for a hundred wintness.

Abhibhūtyojāḥ: of overpowering energy. Vanvan: one who kills enemies. Avātaḥ: unharmed by enemies; this is the form of the root van with the negative prefix. Or else another explanation is given with the sense "unapproached".⟨NOTE:319⟩ Purūhūtaḥ: invoked by many. The words "who is Indra" are to be supplied. O Bharadvāja, praise him, that very Indra; and, further, make that Indra grow with these praises about to be spoken, which are in the form of hymns. What kind of Indra? Unsubdued; fierce, that is, vehement or full of vigour; overcoming, that is, overpowering enemies; the showerer, who belongs to the peoples.
notes: ತ್ಯತ್—ಕರ್ಮಗಳಿಂದ ಪ್ರಸಿದ್ಧನಾದವನು in the Kannada gloss; Sāyaṇa takes tyat as a synonym of tat

en: - वृषभं (*vṛṣabhaṃ*)—the Indra who grants what is desired
- अभिः गीर्भिः (*abhiḥ gīrbhiḥ*)—with these same praises

Praise that very Indra who has vigour that overpowers enemies, who destroys enemies, who is unharmed by anyone and who is invoked by many. With these same praises make grow that Indra who is irresistible, fierce, possessed of power to face enemies and the granter of what is desired to the peoples.

Praise him who is Indra, the invoked of many, endowed with overpowering vigour, the destroyer (of foes), unharmed by them; exalt with these praises the irresistible, fierce, victorious Indra, the showerer (of benefits) upon mankind.

Bṛhadreṇu: the raiser of great dust, that is, in battles. Ekaḥ: the chief. Sahāvā: strong. That Indra became the one who comes upon the Mānuṣī Kṛṣṭis, the peoples belonging to Manu, that is, the yajamānas. What kind of Indra? Yudhma: the warrior. Satvā: the giver. Khajakṛt: the maker of khajas, battles; "khaja" is a name for battle. Samadvā: he who has joy together with the yajamānas. Tuvimrakṣaḥ: one of whom it is said that, by the showering of the many (tuvi), he accomplishes the destruction of foes.⟨NOTE:320⟩ Nadanumān: the noisy one. Ṛjīṣī: by the word "ṛjīṣa" is meant the Soma pressed at the two pressings, and again pressed at the third pressing; he who has it.
notes: ತೈ. ಸಂ ೨ ೧-೧-೧ printed: reference unclear

en: - समद्वा (*samadvā*)—he who rejoices with the yajamānas
- ऋजीषीः (*ṛjīṣīḥ*)—who has Soma whose juice is spent
- बृहद्रेणुः (*bṛhadreṇuḥ*)—who raises great dust in battles

Indra, who is a warrior, a generous giver, the maker of battles, who rejoices with the yajamānas, the helper of many, the noisy one, the possessor of Soma whose juice is spent, raises great dust in battles, is the chief and is possessed of power, and has become the protector of the peoples belonging to Manu.

He is ever the combatant, the donor, the engaged in battle, the sympathizer (with the sacrificer), the benefactor of many, the loud-sounding, the partaker of the stale libation, the stirrer up of dust (in strife), the chief protector of men, the descendants of Manu, the endowed with strength.

O Indra, such as you are: "tyat" is a synonym of "tat", "that", and there is a change of gender here. You quickly tamed the Dasyus, the people devoid of rites; that is, you made them subdued. The word "ha" is a filler. And you, the chief, gave to the Ārya, the man who performs rites, the Kṛṣṭis, that is, sons, servants and the like. The seer, praising Indra in this way, did not see him; doubting then the existence of his valour, he speaks the second half of the Ṛk. O Indra, that valour of yours which was spoken of before: does it exist? The word "svit" here is used in the sense of doubt. Or does it not exist? In either case, declare that strength specially, in season after season.⟨NOTE:321⟩
notes: references printed ೧೦ ೧೦೮-೧೦; ೧೦-೧ ೮-೧೧; ೮_೪೫-೧೪; ೧೦-೯೨-೯೩ with spaces, underscore or odd digit grouping; kept as printed

en: - त्यत् (*tyat*)—he who is famous by his deeds
- त्वं हि नु (*tvaṃ hi nu*)—are you not he?
- दस्यून् (*dasyūn*)—the Dasyu people, who are without rites
- एकः (*ekaḥ*)—you who are chief of all
- आर्याय (*āryāya*)—to the Ārya engaged in rites
- तत् वीर्यं (*tat vīryaṃ*)—that power described before
- स्विन्नु अस्ति (*svinnu asti*)—does it really exist?
- नास्ति स्वित् (*nāsti svit*)—or does it not?

O Indra, your fame has spread everywhere through your deeds. You have subdued the Dasyu people, who are without rites. You, the chief of all, have given sons and other peoples to the Ārya who is engaged in rites. O Indra, does that power of yours, described all along before, really exist in you, or does it not? If it does, make that power of yours manifest according to each season.
You are he who has quickly humbled the Dasyus ; you are the chief one who has given posterity to the Arya; but Indra, is not verily your power such ? if it be not, then in due season confess.

In the previous mantra the seer doubted whether Indra's strength exists; with this one he states with certainty that the strength does indeed exist. The word "hi" is used in the sense of "because". Because, O most mighty Indra, born, that is, manifest at many sacrifices, hostile to those who harm us, or a destroyer of enemies, or strong, I hold that your strength exists. Of you who are fierce, vigorous, grown great, and who cannot be brought under control by enemies, and who are the destroyer of the rivals who are to be subdued, the strength is, and is indeed: of what kind? Fierce, that is, uplifted, and more grown. Since you slay Vṛtra and other enemies, the meaning is that your strength exists indeed.
- तुरतः (*turataḥ*)—to the enemy who harms us
- तुरस्य (*turasya*)—and are the one who inflicts harm

O most powerful Indra, I believe that your strength, you who appear at many sacrifices and inflict harm on the enemy who harms us, is real. Your strength, you who are terrible, powerful and unresisted, is exceedingly terrible, exceedingly powerful and destructive of enemies.

Yet, most mighty one, I believe that power is verily always in you who are manifest at many rites, and are the enemy of (our) enemies; (the power) that is fierce in the fierce one, most mighty in the mighty one, most unassailable in the subduer (of foes).

Pratna means ancient, that is, continuing for a long time. May that famous friendship of ours, the friendship of the praised and the praiser, be in you, O Indra; the plural "yuṣṭe" is used for honour.

O mover of the unmoved, that is, the shaker of those who are unshaken; O handsome Indra, you slew Vala, the Asura who hurled weapons, together with the Aṅgirases who truly praised you. And you opened the cities of this Vala; the meaning is that you made them separate, divided. And you opened all the gates of the cities.
- अच्युतच्युत् (*acyutacyut*)—you who make unmoving mountains and the like move
- इषयंतं (*iṣayaṃtaṃ*)—who was striking with a weapon
- दुरः (*duraḥ*)—the gates of the city also (you have split)

O Indra, may our ancient and famous friendship with you be lasting. O Indra, you who make unmoving mountains and the like move, and are attractive: you have truly slain the Asura Vala, who was striking with a weapon, together with the Aṅgirases who were praising you. You have destroyed the cities of this same Vala. You have split open all the gates of the city.

May that our ancient friendship with you ever endure, as when along with the Angirasas, celebrating your praises, you beautiful Indra, caster down of the immoveable (rocks), slew Vala hurling (his darts against you), and forced open his cities, and all his gates.

The Asura named Vala stole the cows of the gods and hid them in a cave. Then Indra, with the help of his army, besieged that cave and released the cows that were in it. This matter is described in the Yajurveda, Tai. Saṃ. 2 1-1-1,⟨NOTE:322⟩ in this way:

इंद्रो वलस्य बिलमपौर्णोत्स य उत्तमः पशुरासीत्तं पृष्ठं प्रति संगृह्योदक्खिदत्तग्ं सहस्रं पशवोनूदायन्त उन्नतोऽभवद्यः पशुकामः स्यात्स एतमैंद्रमुन्नतमा लभेतेंद्रमेव स्वेन भागधेयेनोप धावति स एवास्मै पशून्प्रयच्छति पशुमानेव भवत्युन्नतो भवति ॥ (*iṃdro valasya bilamapaurṇotsa ya uttamaḥ paśurāsīttaṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ prati saṃgṛhyodakkhidattagṃ sahasraṃ paśavonūdāyanta unnato 'bhavadyaḥ paśukāmaḥ syātsa etamaiṃdramunnatamā labheteṃdrameva svena bhāgadheyenopa dhāvati sa evāsmai paśūnprayacchati paśumāneva bhavatyunnato bhavati ‖*) **GLOSS**

This matter is described here and there in other mantras of the Ṛgveda and in the other Vedas. In the Ṛgveda this matter of Vala is mentioned in the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-62-4; 2-11-20; 2-14-3; 2-15-8; 2-12-3; 2-24-3; 3-30-10; 3-34-10; 4-50-5; 6-18-5; 6-39-2; 8-14-7; 8-24-30; 10-62-2; 10-67-6; 10-68-5; 10-68-6; 10-68-9; 10-68-10; 10-138-1. It is customary to call the soldiers of this Vala Paṇis. It is said in many places that they used to steal cows and hide them in caves.

Although in the Ṛgveda the word "paṇi" has the meaning of wealthy men who carry on trade and the like, it also has the meaning of a man who does not perform sacrifices and the like and does not give sacrificial fees, gifts and so on; therefore the seers appear to have regarded him with contempt, as one not worthy of respect, a base man. In some places the Paṇi seems to be a particular individual, but since the plural use of this word is especially common, it should be understood that "paṇi" indicates a class of people.

The commentator has cited a story about the Paṇis. Rākṣasas called Paṇis stole the cows that were in the world of the gods and hid them in the cave of a mountain. To search for them Indra sent Saramā, the divine bitch (a female dog of the world of the gods). That bitch went to the Paṇis, made them friends with kind words, and helped in bringing the cows. It is said in this story that Indra, with the help of the Maruts, destroyed that mountain cave and brought the cows that were there. In the 108th sūkta of the tenth maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā the conversation that took place on this matter between the divine bitch Saramā and the Rākṣasas called Paṇis is given in detail.

Some are of the opinion that these Paṇis were the earlier inhabitants of this country and were engaged in trade and the like. Since they did not perform sacrifices, had no interest in any good rite, regarded the earning of wealth alone, by fair or unfair means, as the main thing and behaved accordingly, the Āryas regarded them as Dasyus and as men of base conduct, and expressed those opinions in the mantras and elsewhere. In any case, in the Ṛgveda these Paṇis are looked upon with contempt. In the Ṛgveda there are many Ṛks about the Paṇis. Among them—
These forms are recited in the Ṛks. ⟨NOTE:323⟩
It is a current saying that these Paṇis were soldiers of the asura named Vala. The matter that they stole cows and hid them in caves is mentioned in many Ṛks.
notes: ಅತಿ ಪ್ರ ಸರ್ಸ್ರೇ explained by Sāyaṇa as ಅತಿಪ್ರಪೇದೇ, while the Kannada gloss has ಅತಿ ಪ್ರಸಸ್ರೇ "extended greatly"
Ṛk number ೭ not printed after the Saṃhitā or the Pada of this Ṛk; numbered 7 between the printed ೬ and ೮

en: Ugra means mighty. Īśānakṛt: he makes the praisers īśāna, that is, capable. That Indra, in the great (prabhūta) vṛtratūrya, which is a name for battle, is to be invoked by the praisers, or by the praises, by those who desire victory; the particle हि (*hi*) only fills out the foot. For the gaining of a son, when a son is the occasion, and when a son's son is the occasion, that Indra is to be invoked. Vajrī means the possessor of the thunderbolt; that Indra becomes one who is to be glorified in a special way, one who is to be extolled by hymns, in the battles. Or else: वितंतसाय्यः (*vitaṃtasāyyaḥ*) means the destroyer of enemies; the root तंतस (*taṃtasa*) has the sense of injuring, and the word is its form in the agent.
- ईशानकृत् (*īśānakṛt*)—and one who makes the praisers capable
- तोकसाता (*tokasātā*)—for the sake of gaining sons
- तनये (*tanaye*)—for the sake of grandsons and others
- सः (*saḥ*)—that same Indra becomes the one invoked

That same Indra, mighty and giver of strength to the praisers, is prayed to by the praisers in a great battle. That same Indra is invoked for the sake of gaining sons and for the sake of grandsons and others. Indra, endowed with the thunderbolt, is exceedingly worthy of worship in battles.

Fierce Indra, maker of rulers, you are he who is to be invoked with praises in a great conflict ; you are he (who is to be invoked) for sons and graddsons, he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who is to be especially glorified in battles.

That Indra, by his deathless, that is, indestructible, name, which bends the enemies, and by his might (majman is a name for strength), has gone beyond the birth of men, that is, their multitude. That Indra, with fame (dyumna), is samokāḥ, of the same dwelling. Further, that Indra with strength (śavas) becomes samokāḥ. And also Indra, the foremost of leaders, with wealth and with ability becomes samokāḥ. ⟨NOTE:324⟩ ⟨NOTE:325⟩
notes: ಶ್ರೀನಸುರಾನ್ printed in the bhāṣya, read here as "asuras"; Sāyaṇa addresses Indra as "you have injured", the Kannada gloss has the third person
ಅರುಸಲ printed, read "six times"; sentence unclear

en: By his might, which is deathless and makes enemies bow, Indra caused the progeny of men to grow. Indra is together with fame, with strength, with wealth and with ability; that is, wealth, strength and the rest are all with Indra himself.
With immortal, foe-humiliating might, he has promoted the (multiplied) birth of mankind ; he, the chief of leaders, dwells in the same dwelling with fame, with strength, with riches, with heroism.

That Indra who is never bewildered in battle, and who is not a producer of what is false or vain, but is sumantunāmā, of the name prajñāna, that is, of renowned name: that Indra, for the falling, that is, the destruction, of the cities belonging to the enemies, and for the death of the enemies, swiftly performs the act; this is the word to be supplied. Likewise you have destroyed the two asuras named Chumuri and Dhuni (the root वृणक्ति (*vṛṇakti*) has the sense of injuring). And you have injured the asuras named Pipru, Śambara and Śuṣṇa. ⟨NOTE:326⟩
notes: abbreviation ವಾಲ. / ವಾಲ printed

en: - न मुहे (*na muhe*)—is not bewildered in battles
- न भूत् (*na bhūt*)—does not become; such a one
- शयथायॆ (*śayathāyè*)—and for the slaying of the enemies
- धुनिं च (*dhuniṃ ca*)—and the asura called Dhuni

That Indra of renowned fame, who is not bewildered in battles and none of whose undertakings is in vain, will strive swiftly for the destruction of the enemy cities and for the slaying of the enemies. That same Indra slew many Rākṣasas called Chumuri, Dhuni, Pipru, Śambara and Śuṣṇa.

He who is never perplexed, who is no engenderer of that which is in vain, whose name is renowned, who promptly (exerts himself) for the overturning of the cities (of the Asuras), and for the destruction (of his foes); you (Indra), have indeed slain Chumuri, Dhuni, Pipru, Sambara and Sushna.

शुष्ण (*śuṣṇa*)—His name occurs about 40 times. He is the chief enemy of Kutsa. For the sake of this Kutsa, or together with Kutsa, Indra uproots Śuṣṇa (4-16-12, 5-29-9, etc.). He has horns (1-33-12). He has eggs (6-10-10, 11), that is, young ones born of eggs (compare 10-12-11); from this Śuṣṇa too may be called a serpent. He hisses (श्वसनः (*śvasanaḥ*) 1-54-5). Six times the epithet अशुष (*aśuṣa*) (swallowing) is applied to him; this epithet is used only of Agni. ⟨NOTE:327⟩ He has strong forts (1-51-11) or a fort (4-30-13); these are moving forts (8-1-28). Indra destroys the forts of Śuṣṇa and releases the waters (1-51-11); having struck Śuṣṇa he gains the reservoir of water (Vāl. 3-8), or, uprooting the line of Śuṣṇa, he wins the heavenly waters (स्वर्वतीः (*svarvatīḥ*)) (8-40-10). ⟨NOTE:328⟩ Four times Śuṣṇa has the epithet कुयव (*kuyava*) (maker of bad grain). Twice the word कुयव (*kuyava*) itself seems to have been used in place of Śuṣṇa (1-103-8, 1-104-3). The result of the battle between Indra and Śuṣṇa may be not only the release of the waters but also the gaining of cows or of the sun (8-85-17). While fighting with Indra, Śuṣṇa moves about in darkness. He is called a son of snow and a dānava (5-32-4). Śuṣṇa is a dānava who keeps amṛta within himself (Kāṭhaka). From the statements above Śuṣṇa may be called a cause of drought. The root शुष् (*śuṣ*), from which the word शुष् (*śuṣ*) comes, means to hiss or to dry; this too supports that he is a cause of drought.

शंबरः (*śaṃbaraḥ*)—This name occurs about twenty times. Śambara is mentioned together with the other demons, and especially with Śuṣṇa, Pipru (1-101-2, 1-103-8, 2-19-6, 6-18-8) and Varcin. When Indra fought against Ahi and Śambara, the Maruts helped him (3 47-4). When he split Śambara, Indra made the very sky tremble (1-54-4). Having searched out Śambara, who lived on a mountain (2-12-11), he hurled him down from the mountain (1-130-7; 6-26-5). Indra hurled the dāsa Śambara, son of Kulitara, from the great mountain (4-30-14). Having understood himself to be a minor deity, he struck Śambara and made him fall from the high region (7-18-20). Ninety (1-130-7), usually ninety-nine (2-19-6, etc.) or a hundred (2-14 6, etc.) forts are under his control. Once this word, with a neuter ending, has the meaning "the forts of Śambara." Bṛhaspati split these and entered the mountain region that was furnished with treasures (2-24-2). Aditigva (1-51-6), usually Divodāsa (2-19-6, etc.), once both (1-130-7, 2-26-3): for these Indra destroys Śambara. ⟨NOTE:329⟩

पिपु (*pipu*)—The enemy of Ṛjiśvan, who is dependent on Indra (Vāl. 1-10); this Ṛjiśvan, having offered soma juice to Indra, obtains help in the battle against Pipru (5-29-11; 10-99-11). Indra, united with Ṛjiśvan (1-181-1, 2; 10-138-3) or for his sake (4-16-13; 6-20-7), defeated Pipru. Under Pipru, who is endowed with the māyās of Ahi, there are many forts. Indra splits these (1-51-5, 6-20-7). Indra slew the dāsa called Pipru and some others and sent forth the waters (8-32-2). When the sun, in the middle of the sky, unyoked his chariot, the Ātman saw the warrior corresponding to Pipru. Indra, united with Ṛjiśvan, destroyed the strong forts of the māyin asura called Pipru (10-138-3). Indra handed over Pipru, who had the form of a wild beast, to Ṛjiśvan; he defeated fifty thousand black people and split the strongholds (4-16-13). Joining with Ṛjiśvan, Indra destroyed the very offspring of the dark-coloured (1111-1). Because he has both the epithets असुर (*asura*) and दास (*dāsa*), some are of the opinion that he may also have been an enemy of men. ⟨NOTE:330⟩

धुनि (*dhuni*) and चुमुरिः (*cumuriḥ*)—Usually the two names come together. Once Chumuri alone has come. Once it is also used as a dvandva (6-20-13); from this it is known how close the connection of the two is. Indra made the two fall into a sleep (2-15-9, 6-20-13, 7-19-4); the same happened to Chumuri alone (6-26-6). Together with Śambara, Pipru, Śuṣṇa and others, Indra destroyed them and demolished their forts.

(6-18-8). For Dabhīti, who had prepared soma juice for him (6-20-13), Indra destroyed both of them, or made them fall asleep (10-113-9), and Dabhīti obtained from the gods the reward fitting his devotion (6-26-6). For Dabhīti Indra made thirty thousand dasyus fall asleep (4-30-21), and for him he bound the dasyus without a rope (2-13-9). And so on.

ಅಶನಿರ್ನ ಭೀಮಾ: Sāyaṇa "as the thunderbolt is terrible, so you"; the Kannada gloss "you, terrible like your thunderbolt weapon"

en: O Indra, you who are endowed with a might that is rising upward (the root अवति (*avati*) has here the sense of motion), that makes the enemies thin, and that is more worthy of praise: for the killing of Vṛtra, that is, for the slaying of the enemies, mount your own chariot. Likewise, in the right hand place your own weapon, the thunderbolt. After that, O Indra of much wealth, approaching the māyās of the asuras, strike them down with force; here the word मंद (*maṃda*) has the sense of killing. ⟨NOTE:331⟩
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ printed

en: - पन्यसा (*panyasā*)—and worthy of praise; you endowed with such power
- पुरुदत्र (*purudatra*)—O Indra, possessor of abundant wealth
- मायाः अभि (*māyāḥ abhi*)—facing the deceits of the enemies

O Indra, you who are endowed with a power of rising speed (growing), destroying enemies and worthy of praise, mount your chariot and sit in it for the destruction of Vṛtra. Lift up and hold the thunderbolt weapon in your right hand. O Indra, possessor of abundant wealth, face all the deceits of the enemies and conquer them completely.

(Endownd) with upward-rising, foe-thinning, and glorified (vigour), ascend your car fcr the destruction of Vritra: take the thunderbolt in your right hand, and baffle, giver of wealth, the devices (of the Asuras).

The word न (*na*) is used in the sense of comparison. As fire burns up a dry, sapless forest, that is, a mass of trees, so, O Indra, your hetī, your thunderbolt, destroys the enemies. He says the same: as the thunderbolt is terrible, so you, fearsome, burn the rakṣas, the Rākṣasa, completely with the thunderbolt. You, Indra, who with a deep weapon that cannot be assailed by enemies, and with a great one (ऋष्ट (*ṛṣṭa*) is a name for "great"), have broken the enemies; who in battle make a sound of the nature of roaring; and who likewise pierce and break evils: you burn down the Rākṣasa; this is the connection with what came before. ⟨NOTE:332⟩
notes: ಪಥಿಭಿಃ: Sāyaṇa "carriers", the Kannada gloss "horses" and the Bhāvārtha "vehicles"

en: - हेतिः (*hetiḥ*)—your thunderbolt weapon too destroys the enemies
- अध्वनयत् (*adhvanayat*)—have made a sound in battle
- अशनिः न भीमा (*aśaniḥ na bhīmā*)—you, terrible like your thunderbolt weapon

O Indra, as fire burns up masses of dried-up trees, so your thunderbolt weapon too destroys the enemies. You who have split the enemies with your great weapon of abundant power, and who, making a sound in battle, have destroyed all sins: you, terrible like your thunderbolt weapon, destroy the Rākṣasas completely.

In like manner as Agni consumes the dry forest, so, Indra, your weapon (destroys your enemies) as (formidable as your) fearful shaft, consume the Rakshasas : you who have crushed them with your resistless and mighty (weapon), have shouted aloud (in the combat) and demolished all evil things.

O Tuvidyumna, Indra of much wealth, O son of strength (सहसः (*sahasaḥ*) is strength): the sonship of strength is established in another Vedic passage: ओजसो जातमुत मन्य एनं (*ojaso jātamuta manya enaṃ*) Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-73-10 **GLOSS** ⟨NOTE:333⟩. You, endowed with wealth, come with thousands, that is, with many, of very strong pathins; the pathins are the carriers, that is, those by which they go. Come facing me. O Puruhūta, Indra invoked by many: of you, to be separated from your strength and the rest, no asura, no one, is able in the least; here नू चित् (*nū cit*) is used in the sense of prohibition. ⟨NOTE:334⟩
notes: ಅನುಕ್ರೀನಾಮ್ಮೇಕಾಹೇ garbled in the bhāṣya; read as the name of an ekāha
ಮಹಾನ್ತ್ಸಪೋನೇತಿ printed in the bhāṣya; the Anuvāda has ಮಹಾನ್ಸಪ್ತೋನಾ

en: - सहसः सूनो (*sahasaḥ sūno*)—and son of strength
- राया (*rāyā*)—you who are endowed with wealth
- पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)—O Indra, to be called by many
- नू चित् ईशे (*nū cit īśe*)—will not be able in the least

O Indra, possessor of abundant wealth and son of strength, you who are endowed with wealth, be gracious and come facing us, accompanied by vehicles that are great in number and of great strength. O Indra, to be called by many, the asura will not be able in the least to separate you from your powers.
Opulent Indra, Son of strength, the invoked of many, whose union (with energy) the impious is unable to disjoion, come down to us with thousands of riches by very powerful conveyauces.

The greatness of Indra, who is of much fame and much wealth, who is grown great, and who is the grinder of the enemies, has gone beyond heaven, the world of light, and earth. Since विरप्यीति (*virapyīti*) is read among the names for "great," and since names are for the most part produced from roots, the root रप्यति (*rapyati*) here denotes excess. Of this Indra, who is of much wisdom and who overcomes the enemies, there is no enemy, no destroyer; there is no counterpart, no equal; he has no support, no one on whom he rests; he alone is the support of all.
- शुविद्युम्नस्य (*śuvidyumnasya*)—of one who has abundant wealth
- फृष्टेः (*phṛṣṭeḥ*)—and destroyer of enemies, of Indra
- प्र ररष्टे (*pra raraṣṭe*)—has spread out more widely
- पुरुमायस्य (*purumāyasya*)—of one who has much wisdom
- प्रतिष्ठिः (*pratiṣṭhiḥ*)—a superior one (a giver of refuge)

The greatness of Indra, who has abundant wealth, is grown great and destroys enemies, has spread out more widely than the world of light and than the earth. There is no one to injure Indra, who has much wisdom and defeats the enemy. There is no one equal to that Indra, nor any giver of refuge endowed with greater qualities. He alone is the greatest, the giver of refuge to all.

The vastness of the affluent, ancient (Indra), the demolisher (of foes), exceeds that of the heaven and earth : there is no antagonist, no counterpart, no recipient of him abounding in wisdom, victorious (in war).

Today, now also, O Indra, the deed done by you shines forth. What is it? It is that you protected Kutsa, the ṛṣi of that name, from the Rākṣasa Śuṣṇa; Āyu, the son of Purūravas, of that name, from the enemies; and Atithigva, that is, Divodāsa, who goes to guests, from Śambara. This is the connection with what precedes. Because the accusative is heard, the suitable verb "you protected" is to be supplied. Further, to this Atithigva just mentioned you gave many thousands of Śambara's treasures: Indra, having slain Śambara, gave his treasures to Divodāsa. Likewise, O Indra, with your bold thunderbolt, having slain Śambara, you raised up from calamities Divodāsa, who was hastening on the earth, with the earth in view.
- अतिथिग्वं (*atithigvaṃ*)—Atithigva (to protect them from their respective enemies)
- यत् (*yat*)—what great deed you have done
- क्षां अभि (*kṣāṃ abhi*)—who had fallen facing the earth
- उत् निनेथ (*ut ninetha*)—you have lifted up (protected)

O Indra, that great deed which you did to protect Kutsa, Āyu and Atithigva from their respective enemies is famous even now. To this Atithigva you have given exceedingly abundant wealth. By your enemy-destroying power you have lifted up and protected Divodāsa, who, swift in going, had fallen facing the earth.

That exploit is celebrated in the present day (which you have) achived for Kutsa, for Ayu, for Atithigvan : to him you have given many thousands (of riches), and you have quickly elevated Turvayana over the earth by your power.
कुत्सं आयुं अतिथिग्वं (*kutsaṃ āyuṃ atithigvaṃ*)—Here the matter of these three persons will be discussed and explained together.

Sāyaṇa's explanation shows that two kinds of meaning can be given here for the word कुत्स (*kutsa*). First, कुत्सं-कर्तनसाधनं (*kutsaṃ-kartanasādhanaṃ*), "the cutting instrument," as an epithet of the thunderbolt; and second, कुत्सं कुत्सनामानं ऋषिं (*kutsaṃ kutsanāmānaṃ ṛṣiṃ*), the ṛṣi named Kutsa. If it is taken to mean the ṛṣi, it becomes praise of Indra that he killed the asura Śuṣṇa and helped Kutsa.

That the relation between Kutsa and Indra is extremely close is known from the descriptions in the Ṛksaṃhitā. The epithet आर्जुनेय (*ārjuneya*) for Kutsa occurs in many places. The word आर्जुनेय (*ārjuneya*) may mean the son of a woman named Arjunī. Or else, अर्जुन इतींद्रस्य नाम । तस्य पुत्रः (*arjuna itīṃdrasya nāma | tasya putraḥ*): Indra has the name Arjuna, and since Kutsa is his son, the epithet Ārjuneya is natural; thus the meaning can be given in another way. To support that Indra has the name Arjuna, Sāyaṇa, in some places,
has cited the Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā mantra एतद्वा इंद्रस्य गुह्यं नाम यदर्जुनः । (*etadvā iṃdrasya guhyaṃ nāma yadarjunaḥ |*) **GLOSS**. But in the Ṛks
अहं कुत्समार्जुनेयं न्यृंजेऽहं कविरुशना पश्यता मा । (*ahaṃ kutsamārjuneyaṃ nyṛṃje 'haṃ kaviruśanā paśyatā mā |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-26-1) **GLOSS**
दासं यच्चुष्णं कुयवं न्यस्मा अरंधय आर्जुनेयाय शिक्षन् । (*dāsaṃ yaccuṣṇaṃ kuyavaṃ nyasmā araṃdhaya ārjuneyāya śikṣan |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-19-2) **GLOSS**
वहत्कुत्समार्जुनेयं शतक्रतुः त्वरद्गंधर्वमस्तृतं । (*vahatkutsamārjuneyaṃ śatakratuḥ tvaradgaṃdharvamastṛtaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-1-11) **GLOSS**

for all the आर्जुनेय (*ārjuneya*) words occurring in them, Sāyaṇa too has explained as अर्जुन्याः पुत्रं कुत्सं । (*arjunyāḥ putraṃ kutsaṃ |*), that is, Kutsa, the son of the woman Arjunī. Since it is said in other Śrutis that the words Arjuna and Ārjunī are connected with Indra, it can be said that the above two explanations give one and the same meaning. For example—
फल्गुनीष्वग्नी आदधीत । एता वा इंद्रनक्षत्रं यत्फलुन्नोऽप्यस्य प्रतिनाम (*phalgunīṣvagnī ādadhīta | etā vā iṃdranakṣatraṃ yatphalunno 'pyasya pratināma*) (Śa. Brā. 2-1-2-1)
इंद्रो भवति यच्च क्षत्रियो यदु च यजमानस्तस्मादाहारिष्टोऽर्जुन इति । (*iṃdro bhavati yacca kṣatriyo yadu ca yajamānastasmādāhāriṣṭo 'rjuna iti |*) (Śa. Brā. 5-4-3-7) **GLOSS**

The Phalgunis are Indra's nakṣatras. There is agreement in the name also: Indra has the name Arjuna, and the Phalgunis too have the name Arjunis; since this is said in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and in other places, it can be said that Kutsa may be called in two ways, as Indra's son and as Arjunī's son. In many places in the Ṛksaṃhitā the relation between Indra and Kutsa is shown by saying that Kutsa conquers his enemies with Indra's help only.
त्वं शुष्णं वृजने पृक्ष आणौ यूने कुत्साय द्युमते सचाहन् । (*tvaṃ śuṣṇaṃ vṛjane pṛkṣa āṇau yūne kutsāya dyumate sacāhan |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-63-3)
कुत्साय यत्र पुरूहूत वन्वञ्छुष्ण मनंतैः परियासि वध्यैः । (*kutsāya yatra purūhūta vanvañchuṣṇa manaṃtaiḥ pariyāsi vadhyaiḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-121-9)
In these Ṛks, and likewise in many other places, there is the description that Indra killed Śuṣṇa to help Kutsa. And,
अहं पितेव वेतसूरभिष्टये तुग्रं कुत्साय स्मदिभं च रंधयं । (*ahaṃ piteva vetasūrabhiṣṭaye tugraṃ kutsāya smadibhaṃ ca raṃdhayaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-49-4)
Indra himself says: "For Kutsa I defeated Vetasu, Tugra, Smadibha and all such enemies, and helped my friend." But,
त्वमस्मै कुत्समतिथिग्वमायुं महे राज्ञे यूने आरंधनायः । (*tvamasmai kutsamatithigvamāyuṃ mahe rājñe yūne āraṃdhanāyaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-53-10)
य आयुं कुत्समतिथिग्वमर्दयो वावृधानो दिवेदिवे । (*ya āyuṃ kutsamatithigvamardayo vāvṛdhāno divedive |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-53-10)
In such Ṛks it is also described that Indra defeated Kutsa and others.

Use: in the ekāha called अनुक्रीनाम्मेकाहे (*anukrīnāmmekāhe*) ⟨NOTE:335⟩, in the Marutvatīya śastra, the verse अनु त्वाहिघ्न (*anu tvāhighna*) is the opening verse of the sūkta. And it is aphorized: अनु त्वाहिघ्ने अध देव देवा अनु ते दायि मह इंद्रियाय । (*anu tvāhighne adha deva devā anu te dāyi maha iṃdriyāya |*) Ā. Sū. 9-5. O shining Indra, at this time all the gods, the praisers, join in praising you for the slaying of Ahi, that is, of the cloud, that is, for the giving of rain. Of what sort are you? The most wise poet among the wise. At the time when you, praised by the praisers, give wealth to the person afflicted by poverty and the like,

to the praising person, and to the descendants of the praisers, you made, that is, gave, wealth. Or else: O Indra, at this time all the gods join in praising you, the most wise of the wise, for the slaying of Ahi, that is, of Vṛtra himself. When this praise is made, to the person who dwells in the world of heaven and was oppressed by the asuras, for his splendour, for your own splendour by the slaying of Vṛtra, you made wealth.
notes: ಸಮೂಳ್ಛೇ printed in the bhāṣya, ಸಮೂಳ್ವ in the Anuvāda; name of the sacrifice doubtful

en: - दिवे जनाय (*dive janāya*)—to the praising folk
- तन्ने (*tanne*)—and to his sons and others
- अनु मदन् (*anu madan*)—gather together and praise

O shining Indra, at the time when you, praised by the praisers, give wealth to the praising folk afflicted by poverty and to their sons and others, at such a time all the praisers, gathering together, praise you, the best poet among poets, for the destruction of Vṛtra.
Divine Indra, all the gods have glorified you, the wisest of the wise, for the destruction of Ahi: when propitiated, you have given wealth to the distressed worshipper, and to his posterity.

O Indra, that famed might of yours, heaven and earth follow. The immortal gods, those who are not subject to death, follow your might, that is, go after it. O doer of many deeds, whatever deed of yours is not yet done, do it. After that, in the sacrifices, bring forth a newer hymn.
- कृत्नो (*kṛtno*)—O Indra, doer of many deeds

O Indra, heaven and earth and the gods have acknowledged your famed might. O Indra, doer of many deeds, now accomplish all those of your deeds that are still not done. In this sacrifice make a new praise.
The heaven and earth, and the immortal gods acknowledge your might : doer of many deeds, do that which is yet undone by you, give birth to a new hymn at (your) sacrifices.

Like a leader, a king, who fulfils wishes such as prosperity, so may Indra, the fulfiller of the wishes of the people who praise him, the great and mighty one, come here. The word "ā" is seen as a preverb, and so the verb "come" is to be supplied. Moreover, Indra, who surpasses in both worlds and who cannot be injured by the forces of his enemies, grows towards us, facing us, for the doing of heroic deeds. He is wide in body and renowned for his qualities, and is well served by the sacrificers.
- नृवत् (*nṛvat*)—as a king fulfils the wishes of his subjects
- चर्षणिप्राः (*carṣaṇiprāḥ*)—fulfiller of the wishes of created beings
notes: ಶೋಕಸ್ಯ in the bhāṣya, where the Ṛk has ತೋಕಸ್ಯ

en: May Indra, who as a king fulfils the wishes of his subjects, is the fulfiller of the wishes of those who praise him, and is great-souled, be gracious. Grown great in heaven and earth and unharmed by the forces of his enemies, he attains growth, facing us, so as to increase our strength. Of vast form and of very abundant qualities, he is honoured by the sacrificer.
May the great Indra, who is as a monarch, the fulfiller (of the desires) of men, come hither: may he who is mighty over the two (realms
of space), uninjurable by (hostile) efforts, increase (in capacity) for heroism in our presence : may he who is great (in body). eminent (in qualities), be honoured by the performers (of pious acts)

अमिनः (*aminaḥ*)—one who is unharmed. Since the strength and valour of Indra are very great, the meaning is that however powerful an enemy may be, he cannot injure Indra. Concerning this word Yāska has given the etymology:
अमिनः । अमिनोऽमितमात्रो महान् भवत्यभ्यमितो वा । अमिनः सहोभिः इत्यपि निगमो भवति ॥ (*aminaḥ | amino 'mitamātro mahān bhavatyabhyamito vā | aminaḥ sahobhiḥ ityapi nigamo bhavati ‖*)

This word अमिनः (*aminaḥ*) is derived from the root माज् माने (*māj māne*) and gives the meaning "one whose strength and valour cannot be measured (immeasurable)". It also means "great", or "one who cannot be injured (invulnerable)". To explain the meaning of this word he has given as example the very Ṛk in hand, अमिनः सहोभिः (*aminaḥ sahobhiḥ*). No one can measure, that is, state definitely and exactly, that the strength and valour of Indra are only so much. His power and capacity are unfathomable. Therefore the chief meaning is that no enemy, of whatever kind, can injure Indra.

द्विबर्हाः (*dvibarhāḥ*)—द्वि (*dvi*) means two, बर्ह (*barha*) means big. Therefore this word means one who has grown exceedingly great in two places, that is, in heaven and in the atmosphere. For this word Yāska has given the etymology:

द्विबर्हाः द्वयोः स्थानयोः परिवृढो मध्यमे च स्थान उत्तमे च । उत द्विबर्हा अमिनः सहोभिः इत्यपि निगमो भवति ॥ (*dvibarhāḥ dvayoḥ sthānayoḥ parivṛḍho madhyame ca sthāna uttame ca | uta dvibarhā aminaḥ sahobhiḥ ityapi nigamo bhavati ‖*)

"In two places" means: in the atmosphere, the middle place, in the form of lightning, and in heaven in the form of the sun, he pervades and shines; this is the meaning. That is, the chief meaning is that the sun shining in the world of heaven and the lightning seen in the atmosphere are both forms of Indra. Here the Ṛk in hand itself, उत द्विबर्हा अमिनः सहोभिः (*uta dvibarhā aminaḥ sahobhiḥ*), is given as the example.
महा इंद्रः (*mahā iṃdraḥ*)—महान् इंद्रः (*mahān iṃdraḥ*). As to how Indra obtained the title Mahān (great), there is an ancient story in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa:

इंद्रो वै वृत्रं हत्वा सर्वा विजितीर्विजित्याब्रवीत्प्रजापतिमहमेतदसानि यत्त्वमहं महानसानीति स प्रजापतिरब्रवीदथ कोऽहमिति यद्यैवैतदवोच इत्यब्रवीत्ततो वै को नाम प्रजापतिरभवत्को वै नाम प्रजापतिर्यन्महानिंद्रोऽभवत्तन्महेंद्रस्य महेंद्रत्वं । (*iṃdro vai vṛtraṃ hatvā sarvā vijitīrvijityābravītprajāpatimahametadasāni yattvamahaṃ mahānasānīti sa prajāpatirabravīdatha ko 'hamiti yadyaivaitadavoca ityabravīttato vai ko nāma prajāpatirabhavatko vai nāma prajāpatiryanmahāniṃdro 'bhavattanmaheṃdrasya maheṃdratvaṃ |*)

In the past, after Indra had slain Vṛtra, he conquered all the regions of the earth and said to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, you have now gained a position of greatness and are venerable. From now on I want your position of greatness." When Prajāpati asked: "If you take my position, then who (kaḥ) am I? What is my standing?", Indra said: "O Prajāpati, as you yourself have just said, your name from now on will be Ka (who); that is, you will be denoted by the word ka." Therefore from that time Prajāpati became denoted by the word ka. This matter is well known. For that reason it is stated in the pratigraha mantras, which are to be recited when one accepts any gift. That is, there is a Brāhmaṇa sentence of the other Vedas:
क इदं कस्मा अदादित्याह । प्रजापतिर्वै कः । प्रजापतॆय एव तद्ददाति (*ka idaṃ kasmā adādityāha | prajāpatirvai kaḥ | prajāpatèya eva taddadāti*) **GLOSS**

Since the word ka has the meaning "happiness", in the usages and matters connected with Prajāpati he is said to be of the nature of happiness. Because Indra thus took over the greatness of Prajāpati, the appellation Mahān came to Indra; that is, Indra became Mahān Indra. This matter is told in the other Vedas also:
इंद्रो वृत्रमहन्तं देवा अब्रुवन्महान्ना अयमभूद्यो वृत्रमवधीदिति तन्महेंद्रस्य महेंद्रत्वं । (*iṃdro vṛtramahantaṃ devā abruvanmahānnā ayamabhūdyo vṛtramavadhīditi tanmaheṃdrasya maheṃdratvaṃ |*)

The gods, praising Indra's slaying of Vṛtra, said: "Because this Indra slew Vṛtra, he has become Mahendra (has gained greatness)"; that is, he became the best of all the gods. It is said that this is the reason why the name Mahendra came to Indra.

स महून्भूत्वा देवता अब्रवीदुद्धारं म उद्धरतेति यथाप्येतर्हिच्छति यो वै भवति यः श्रेष्ठतामश्नुते स महान्भवति तं देवा अब्रुवन् स्वयमेव ब्रूष्ट यत्ते भविष्यतीति स एतं माहेंद्रं ग्रहमब्रूत माध्यंदिनं सवनानां निष्केवल्यमुक्थानां त्रिष्टुभं छंदसां पृष्ठं साम्नां तमस्मा उद्धारमुदहरन् उदस्मा उद्धारं हरंति य एवं वेद । (*sa mahūnbhūtvā devatā abravīduddhāraṃ ma uddharateti yathāpyetarhicchati yo vai bhavati yaḥ śreṣṭhatāmaśnute sa mahānbhavati taṃ devā abruvan svayameva brūṣṭa yatte bhaviṣyatīti sa etaṃ māheṃdraṃ grahamabrūta mādhyaṃdinaṃ savanānāṃ niṣkevalyamukthānāṃ triṣṭubhaṃ chaṃdasāṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ sāmnāṃ tamasmā uddhāramudaharan udasmā uddhāraṃ haraṃti ya evaṃ veda |*)

Then Indra, having gained the position of greatness as stated above, called the gods and spoke thus: "O gods, since I have gained a position of greatness, arrange on this account, that is, to felicitate me, some honourable reception." In worldly usage also, when a man obtains incomparable prosperity, or distinction in learning and the like, or royal honour, such a man is famed as esteemed among people, and so it is the custom that people arrange a reception to felicitate him. In the same way Indra put this question to the gods. The gods also approved Indra's word and said: "O Indra, how should this reception be arranged? How would you be pleased? You yourself must say it; we shall act accordingly." To this Indra said: "Among the grahas (a graha is a special vessel for drinking soma), the Mahendra graha (the soma-drinking vessel offered to me, Mahendra) must be the best of all grahas. In the same way, among the three savanas, the Prātaḥ-savana, the Mādhyandina savana and the third savana, the Mādhyandina savana; among the śastras (mantras) such as the Āśvina śastra and the Marutvatīya, the Niṣkevalya śastra; among the metres such as Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭup metre; among the sāmans, the Bṛhad-rathantara sāman which produces the Pṛṣṭha stotra, must be the best; you must approve this. For all of these are dear to me. This is the honour you will do me." The gods agreed that it should be so, and approved the pre-eminence of the Māhendra graha and the others in sacrifices. This matter is said in the other Vedas also:

स एतं माहेंद्रमुदहरत वृत्रं हत्वान्यासु देवतास्वधीति यन्माहेंद्रो गृह्यत उद्धारमेव तं यजमान उद्धरते न प्रजास्वधि । (*sa etaṃ māheṃdramudaharata vṛtraṃ hatvānyāsu devatāsvadhīti yanmāheṃdro gṛhyata uddhārameva taṃ yajamāna uddharate na prajāsvadhi |*)
The sacrificer who knows this matter will gain pre-eminence among people and an esteemed position.

Dhiṣaṇā is our praise. For the sake of giving it holds Indra alone, Indra of this kind: great, going (quick-moving), ageless, free from old age, ever young, grown great with unsurpassed strength that is not overcome by enemies. Indra, as soon as he was born, grew mightily, in a way that is not small.

Indra, who grew exceedingly as soon as he was born, is of great form, swift-moving, free from old age, ever young, and attains greatness by his unobstructed strength. Our praise approaches that Indra alone, for the sake of giving.
Our praise encourages Indra to munificence, the vast, quick-moving, undecaying, ever-youthful Indra, mighty with unsurpassable strength, who rapidly grows to greatness.

O Indra, extend your two arms, wide, doers of deeds and bountiful, towards us, facing us, to give food; the word "to give" is to be supplied, and by श्रवांसि (*śravāṃsi*) foods are meant. Further, O Indra, with a tamed mind, turn towards us in battle, as an example, as a herdsman, the protector of cattle, turns round the herds of cattle.
- यूथेव (*yūtheva*)—as he surrounds and protects the herds
- अभि आ ववृत्स्व (*abhi ā vavṛtsva*)—stand around us and protect

O Indra, extend towards us, facing us, your two arms, wide, doers of deeds and exceedingly bountiful, so as to give us food. O Indra, as a herdsman surrounds and protects the herds of cattle, so do you, of tamed mind, stand around us in battle and protect us.
Extend towards us your long, active, and bountiful hands, (to bring us) food : be about us, lowly-minded indra, in battle, as a herdsman (tends) the herds of cattle.

Today, here at this sacrifice, we singers, desiring food, call upon Indra, the supreme lord, the well-known one, who together with his able and powerful helpers the Maruts is the destroyer of enemies; the word cātaka here means destroyer. We praise you. Just as the ancient singers were blameless, free from reproach, free from sin and unharmed, so, O Indra, by your grace may we also become the same.
- अस्य शाकैः (*asya śākaiḥ*)—together with the Maruts, the helpers of Indra
notes: ವಿಶ್ವಸಹಂ—ಲೋಕವನ್ನೆಲ್ಲಾ ನಿಯಮಿಸುವವನೂ; Sāyaṇa glosses it "overcomer of the whole world"

en: In this sacrifice we, who desire food, praise Indra, the destroyer of enemies and the well-known one, together with his helpers the Maruts. O Indra, in the manner in which our ancestors were singers of praise, blameless, free from sin and non-injuring, so may we also become.

Desiring sustenance, we invoke you, the renowned Indra, on this occasion, the destroyer (of enemies), together with his powerful allies (the Maruts): as his ancient adorers have been, (may we be), exempt from blame, irreproachable, unharmed.

That Indra indeed is the one who keeps his vows, that is, who bears his deeds, and he alone is the giver of wealth. Of what kind of wealth? To meet that question the qualifying words are given, even though the wealth is a subordinate member: of desirable, that is, to-be-wished-for, best wealth. Or else, the words "lord of wealth" are to be supplied. He alone is grown strong through Soma, and he alone is rich in food. In him, Indra alone, the riches that are beneficial to the singers come together. The example: as rivers, flowing together, approach the ocean, so riches come to him.
- स हि (*sa hi*)—that well-known Indra himself
- धृतव्रतः (*dhṛtavrataḥ*)—is one whose appointed work is regularly undertaken
- पुरुक्षुः (*purukṣuḥ*)—and possessed of exceeding abundance of food
- सिंधवः न (*siṃdhavaḥ na*)—as all rivers enter together
- पथ्याः (*pathyāḥ*)—that do good to the singers

That well-known Indra is one whose appointed work is regularly undertaken, and the giver of attractive and excellent wealth. He is grown strong by drinking Soma and is possessed of exceeding abundance of food. As all the rivers that go into the ocean enter the ocean together and become one, so all the riches that are beneficial to the singers come together in this Indra.

In him who is observant of pious rites, who is a giver of wealth, who is exalted by the Soma beverage, the (lord) of desirable riches, the distributor of food, (in him) the treasures fit (for his worshippers) congregate like rivers flowing into the ocean.

O valiant, mighty Indra, bring to us the most powerful strength. O Indra, overcomer of enemies, bring to us fierce, irresistible, most vigorous vigour, brilliance. O Indra, lord of bay horses, grant to us, for our delight, all those shining riches, able to shower their benefits, which have been appointed as the enjoyment of men.
- ओजिष्ठं (*ojiṣṭhaṃ*)—and endowed with the utmost vigour
- हरिवः (*harivaḥ*)—O Indra, who have the horses named Hari

O valiant Indra, grant us strength of the utmost might. O Indra, subduer of enemies, provide us also with inner power that is terrible to enemies and endowed with the utmost vigour. O Indra, who have the horses named Hari, give us, for our satisfaction, all the riches that are beneficial to men and satisfying.

Bestow upon us, hero Indra, most vigorous vigour: subduer (of enemies, bestow upon us) most energetic and fierce energy: grant, lord of steeds, all the bright and invigorating (treasures) fit for men, to make us happy.

Pṛtanāṣāṭ is the overcomer of the armies of enemies; amṛdhra is unharmed. O Indra, that joy of yours which is to be given by you, which is grown to abundance, bring to us. We, protected by you and victorious, for the winning of a son and a grandson, with which joy we may praise you, bring that: this is the connection with the earlier words. ⟨NOTE:340⟩
notes: ಸಂಹಿತಾಪಾಠ ends ॥ ೩ ॥ while the Padapāṭha and the series give ೧೩

en: - अमृध्रः (*amṛdhraḥ*)—and is unharmed by the enemy
- यः मदः (*yaḥ madaḥ*)—which joy there is
- त्वोताः (*tvotāḥ*)—we who are protected by you
- तोकस्य सात् (*tokasya sāt*)—for the sake of a son
- तनयस्य (*tanayasya*)—and for the sake of a grandson

O Indra, that joy which overcomes enemies and is unharmed by the enemy, and which is given by you and of abundant measure, that same joy provide to us also, we who, protected by you and desiring victory, with that joy shall praise you for the sake of our grandsons and the rest.

Impart to us, Indra, that your invigorating exultation which overcomes enemies, and is irresistible, whereby, protected by you, triumphant we may glorify you for the sake of (obtaining) sons and grandsons.

O Indra, bring to us the showering strength, which has the form of an army: of what kind? Protector of wealth, grown great, of good skill, that is, of fine strength. O Indra, with your protections, in battles (pṛtanā is a name for battle), with which strength we may slay our enemies. In the word "uta" the order is different: with which strength we may slay kinsmen and also enemies who are not kinsmen, bring that strength; the connection is with the earlier words.
- जामिन् (*jāmin*)—whether in the form of kinsmen
- धनस्पृतं (*dhanaspṛtaṃ*)—and such as protects our wealth

O Indra, with your protections, provide us in battles the strength by which we are able to slay all our enemies, that is, whether they be in the form of kinsmen or not kinsmen, all of them; and which protects our wealth, is to be increased, possesses excellent capacity and bestows what is desired.

Bestow upon us, Indra, vigorous strength, the realizer of wealth, great and propitious, wherewith, through your protection, we may destroy our enemies in battles, whether they be kinsmen or strangers.

O Indra, may your strength, the showerer of benefits, come towards us from the western quarter; may it come from the northern quarter; may it come from the lower, that is the southern, quarter; and may it come from the eastern quarter. May it come to us from every quarter, aiming at us, and unite with us fully. O Indra, grant us wealth that is joined with happiness.
- आ समेतु (*ā sametu*)—may it come and join us

O Indra, may your strength, which showers desires and is related to you, come to us, facing us, from the western quarter, from the northern quarter, and also from the eastern and southern quarters. May that strength come from all quarters and join us. O Indra, give us wealth that is joined with happiness and productive of happiness.
May your invigorating strength come from the west, from the north, from the south, from the east; may it come to us from every quarter: grant us riches combined with felicity.

O Indra, we would enjoy, from you, with your best-guiding protections, wealth that is desirable, accompanied by men, that is, by attendants, and by renowned fame to be heard of. Because, O shining king Indra, you rule over both kinds of wealth, that of the earth and that of heaven, for that reason give us great, vast wealth, surpassing in its qualities, delightful.
- नृवत् (*nṛvat*)—and accompanied by sons and the like
- उभयस्य (*ubhayasya*)—belonging to both heaven and earth
- ईक्षे (*īkṣe*)—you are the master (for that very reason)

O Indra, may we enjoy the wealth that is given by you, joined with guiding protections, accompanied by sons and the like, joined with fame, and attractive. O lord Indra, because you are the master of all the wealth that belongs to both heaven and earth, for that very reason give us wealth that is great, vast, of exceeding qualities and delightful.

We enjoy, Indra, through your guiding protection, desirable affluence along with descendants and reputation: grant us, sovereign, you rule over (earthly and heavenly) riches, vast, desirablr, and infinite treasure.

ईक्षे (*īkṣe*)—Concerning this word Yāska has given the etymology: ईक्ष ईशिषे । ईक्षे हि वस्व उभयस्य राजन् इत्यपि निगमो भवति (*īkṣa īśiṣe | īkṣe hi vasva ubhayasya rājan ityapi nigamo bhavati*) (Ni. 6-7). The word ईक्षे (*īkṣe*) has the same meaning as the word ईशिषे (*īśiṣe*), that is, "you exercise lordship, you rule a kingdom". Here the Ṛk in hand itself is given as the example. The meaning of this sentence is: O Indra, the king, you are the lord of all the wealth that lies in the two worlds, heaven and earth.

Here, in this sacrifice, for new, that is fresh, protection we call upon, that is, we praise or invite, that well-known Indra. Of what kind is he? Attended by the Maruts; the showerer of desires; grown great; one whose enemy is not contemptible; shining; the ruler; the overcomer of the whole world; fierce, that is, mighty; the giver of strength.
- मरुत्वंतं (*marutvaṃtaṃ*)—who is accompanied by the Maruts
- अकवारिं (*akavāriṃ*)—not to be reviled by enemies
- इह (*iha*)—at this time of the sacrifice
notes: Ṛk number ೨ not printed at the end of the Pada-pāṭha; number 2 taken from the sequence

en: At this time of the sacrifice we pray and call, for fresh protection, that well-known Indra, who is accompanied by the Maruts, the showerer of desires, grown great, not to be reviled by enemies, shining, lord, controller of the world, terrible, and the giver of strength.

We invoke on this occasion for his present protection, that Indra who is attended by the Maruts; who is the showerer (of benefits); augmenting (in powess); the unreviled of foes, radiant, ruling, all-subduing, fierce, the giver of strength.

O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, subdue that person among the men in whose number I am one, who thinks himself exceedingly great, that is, who thinks highly of himself. The word चित् (*cit*) serves to fill out the verse-line. Now, on the earth, when a battle has begun, for the sake of a son, and for the sake of cattle and of water, O Indra, we call upon you who are stationed in the world of heaven.
- वज्रिन् (*vajrin*)—O Indra, bearer of the thunderbolt weapon
- एभ्यः नृभ्यः (*ebhyaḥ nṛbhyaḥ*)—in such a company of men
- महि मन्यमानं (*mahi manyamānaṃ*)—who thinks himself the greatest and is proud
- तनये (*tanaye*)—for the sake of a son

O Indra, bearer of the thunderbolt, subdue that person who, in the company of men among whom I am also one, thinks himself the greatest and is proud. Now, on the earth, when battle has come, we pray to you for the sake of a son, for the sake of cattle, and for the sake of water.

Wielder of the thunderbolt, humble that man who looks upon himself as the greatest amongst those men of whom I am : we invoke you now to (descend) upon the earth at the time of battle, and for (the sake of obtaining) sons and grandsons.

notes: ಯಜೀಷಿನ್ printed; the Ṛk has ಋಜೀಷಿನ್

en: O Indra, invoked by many, with these well-known friendly acts, which have the form of praises, together with you, we, striking both kinds of enemies, those of the form of kinsmen and those of the form of non-kinsmen, would be superior to every enemy; that is, we would become the greater. O valiant Indra, protected by you, may we rejoice with great wealth.
- पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)—O Indra, who are called by many
- उत्तरे इत् (*uttare it*)—in a very superior position

O Indra, who are called by many, may we, joined with you by your well-known friendly acts, be in a position superior to all enemies, striking all forms of our enemies, both kinsmen and non-kinsmen. O valiant Indra, protected by you, may we rejoice with exceeding wealth.

Invoked of many, may we, through these your friendly (praises), ever be superior to successive foes, destroying, oh hero, both (classes of) enemies, (kindred or unallied); and may we, protected by you, be happy with abundant riches.

The riches in the form of a son, which with strength attacks the enemy people in battles, as the shining sun overspreads all beings. O Indra, son of strength, give us that son: one who bears a thousand-fold wealth, who enjoys lands rich in crops, who overcomes enemies in battle.
- सहसः सूनो (*sahasaḥ sūno*)—O son of strength
- द्यौः न (*dyauḥ na*)—as the sun overspreads with his rays
- यः रयिः (*yaḥ rayiḥ*)—which wealth in the form of a son
- आर्यः जनान् (*āryaḥ janān*)—all the enemy people
- उर्वरासां (*urvarāsāṃ*)—enjoying the earth filled with all crops and the like
- वृत्रतुरं (*vṛtraturaṃ*)—destroying enemies, the riches in the form of a son

O Indra, son of strength, as the sun overspreads all beings with his rays, so the wealth in the form of a son which with its strength overspreads all the enemy people in battle: such wealth in the form of a son, bearing a thousand-fold riches, enjoying the earth filled with all crops and the like, and destroying enemies, grant to us.

Indra, Son of strength, grant us (a son), the possessor of thousands, the owner of cultivated lands, the subduer of foes, the riches that may overcome men in battles by strength, as the radiant (sun) overspreads the earth by his rays.

In this Ṛk there is no proper word for the subject. Although the word रयिः (*rayiḥ*) means wealth, the bhāṣyakāra has explained it as wealth in the form of a son and has supplied that in the place of the subject word. Although no qualities that define a son are stated here, the epithet वृत्रतुरं (*vṛtraturaṃ*), "destroyer of enemies", supports the bhāṣyakāra's explanation to some extent.

notes: ಪ್ರರಿಕ್ತಾನತಿರಿಕ್ತಾನ್ನಾಕರೋತ್ construction unclear; ಬಲೇಃ for ಬಲೈಃ

en: As to the sun, O Indra, to you all-pervading strength has truly been given by the gods, the praisers; the meaning is that the deity who is praised by the praisers becomes mighty. O Indra, whose soma has lost its juice, associated with Viṣṇu: by which strength you slew Vṛtra the Asura, the enemy who came and enclosed the waters, that strength was given; thus it is connected with what precedes.
- ऋजीषिन् इंद्र (*ṛjīṣin iṃdra*)—O Indra, who have the soma called ṛjīṣa
- दिवो न (*divo na*)—as all powers are placed in the sun

O Indra, who drink the soma called ṛjīṣa, joined with Viṣṇu: the strength by which you killed Vṛtra, who obstructed the waters, has been truly entrusted to you by all the gods, as all powers are placed in the sun.
To you, Indra, as to the sun, all strength has verily been given by the gods; so that, drinker of the stale Soma, associated with Vishnu, you might slay the hostile Ahi obstructing waters.

यजीषिन् (*yajīṣin*)⟨NOTE:344⟩—we have already explained the meaning of this word earlier. After the soma plants are crushed with stones and the juice is pressed out, the husks that remain are called ऋजीष (*ṛjīṣa*). The little juice that is in them is pressed out once more, barley flour is mixed with it, and it is offered to Indra at the third pressing. Therefore, that is, because he drinks the soma juice that is in the ṛjīṣa, it is customary to call Indra Ṛjīṣin.
notes: ಮಾರಲವಕಾಶ printed; ಮೀರಲವಕಾಶ?

en: When Indra took the vajra, the cleaver of all the cities, then he became the lord of the sweet juice of soma, he who is the destroyer of the harmful, exceedingly vigorous, stronger than the strong, one for whom the praisers have made praise, or else one by whom food has been given to the praisers, and one of grown splendour. Such an Indra became king.
- कृतब्रह्मा (*kṛtabrahmā*)—one for whom praise has been made in his honour

Indra, who is the destroyer of enemies, vigorous, possessed of greater strength than all the mighty, one for whom praise has been made in his own honour, and one of grown splendour: when he took in his hand the vajra weapon that destroys all the enemy cities, then he became the lord of the sweet soma juice.

When Indra, the destroyer, the most mighty, the strongest of the strong, the giver of food, the possessor of vast splendour. received (the thunderbolt), the shatterer of all the cities (of the Asuras), he became the lord of the sweet Soma beverage.

Here, in this battle fought for food (arka is food, and the battle in which food is obtained is so called), because of the wise one with abundant oblations, Kutsa, the fourth case being used in the sense of the fifth. O Indra, the Paṇis, Asuras of that name, fearing Kutsa, who was your helper, fled with their hundreds of forces. And Indra did not leave over the deceptions of Śuṣṇa, the Asura of that name, the enemy of Kutsa, of the unwithered, that is, of full strength, with his weapons, the instruments of slaying; he made them not left over. Pitu is a name of food: he did not leave even a little of his food, he carried all his food away. ⟨NOTE:345⟩
notes: ಮಾರದಿರುವಂತೆ printed; ಮೀರದಿರುವಂತೆ?

en: - अत्र अर्कसातौ (*atra arkasātau*)—in this battle fought for the sake of food
- अशुषस्य (*aśuṣasya*)—of the one of full strength
- वध्यैः (*vadhyaiḥ*)—having checked with his own weapons, the instruments of slaying
- न प्र अरिरेचीत् (*na pra arirecīt*)—destroyed his power without giving it any opening⟨NOTE:346⟩
- किंचन प्र (*kiṃcana pra*)—carried off everything, without any remainder
notes: ಇತ್ಯಸಯೋಚ್ಯತ ಇತಿ at the end of the Sāyaṇa block damaged

en: O Indra, in this battle fought for the sake of food, the Paṇis, fearing Kutsa, who has abundant oblations and is wise, fled. For their flight, your very strength that protects Kutsa

is the cause. Indra, checking with his own weapons of slaying the deceptions of the Asura named Śuṣṇa, who had full strength, destroyed him so that his power might not prevail⟨NOTE:347⟩. He carried off all his food, leaving not a little remainder.
notes: ಸ್ವಸ್ವವಿನಾಶೇನ in the Sāyaṇa block unclear; the gloss has ಸ್ವಸ್ತಿ "imperishable"

en: The Panis, Indra, fled, with hundreds (of Asuras), from the sage, your worshipper (and ally) in battle: neither did he, (Indra), suffer the decptions of the powerful Sushna to prevail over his weapons, nor did he (leave him) any of his sustenance.

In this Ṛk and in the next Ṛk the matter is described that Indra, in order to help Kutsya, killed the Asura named Śuṣṇa and in battle scattered and put to flight his soldiers, the Asuras called Paṇis. That Indra slew Śuṣṇa only for the sake of helping Kutsya is stated in many Ṛks:
त्वं शुष्णं वृजने पृक्ष आणौ यूने कुत्साय द्युमते सचाहन् । (*tvaṃ śuṣṇaṃ vṛjane pṛkṣa āṇau yūne kutsāya dyumate sacāhan |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-63-3) **GLOSS**
कुत्साय यत्र पुरुहूत वन्वञ्छुष्ण मनंतैः परियासि वधैः । (*kutsāya yatra puruhūta vanvañchuṣṇa manaṃtaiḥ pariyāsi vadhaiḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-121-9) **GLOSS**
In these Ṛks, and likewise in the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-174-5; 1-175-4 and others, it is said that Indra killed Śuṣṇa in order to help Kutsya. And further:
अहं पितेव वेतसूरभिष्टये तुग्रं कुत्साय स्मदिभं च रंधयं । (*ahaṃ piteva vetasūrabhiṣṭaye tugraṃ kutsāya smadibhaṃ ca raṃdhayaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-49-4)
Indra himself declares: "For Kutsa I overcame Vetasu, Tugra and Smṛdibha."

When that Asura Śuṣṇa fell at the falling of the vajra, that is, was killed, then the all-pervading strength belonging to Śuṣṇa, the great harmer, was put away, that is, set aside. That Indra, for Kutsa, who was his charioteer, made the chariot a common chariot, widened, for the sake of the worship of the sun. And so it is said: Indra, wishing to slay the Asura Śuṣṇa for Kutsa, made Kutsa his own charioteer, slew his enemy Śuṣṇa, and thereby gave Kutsa abundant protection. ⟨NOTE:348⟩
