O Indra, possessor of might, whatever protection of yours is the lowest, whatever is the highest and most excellent, and whatever is the middle one, with all those protections protect us thoroughly in the battle with Vṛtra, that is, in war. Further, O fierce Indra, who have raised your weapon, you are great: the word "unite" is to be supplied, so that the sense is: unite us with these foods, the means of enjoyment.
- वृत्रहत्ये (*vṛtrahatye*)—in the battle that destroys the enemy

O powerful Indra, with your protections of many kinds, whether they are the most excellent, or of middling degree, or ordinary, with all those protections protect us greatly in the battle that destroys the enemy. O Indra of surpassing might, you of great form, make us endowed with wealth by these foods that are fit for enjoyment.

Powerful Indra, with these (your protections), whether the protection be little, great, or middling, defend us for the destruction of our foes: supply us, fierce Indra, who are mighty, with those viands (that are needed).

O Indra, with these our praises, our armies, which smite the hosts of the enemy, protecting them without harming them, crush the wrath of the enemy, the anger that exists in battles and the like. Further, with these very praises destroy for the Ārya, the sacrificer who performs rites such as sacrifice, all the peoples who confront us, who are spread everywhere, and who are the servile ones, destroyers of rites ⟨NOTE:392⟩.
notes: ಆನುಕ್ರೀನಾಮ್ಯೇಕಾಹೇ: the machine reading is damaged; the Kannada Anuvāda reads ಅನುಕ್ರೀ ಎಂಬ ಏಕಾಹಯಾಗ

en: - अभिः (*abhiḥ*)—with the help of these praises recited by us
- मिथतीः (*mithatīḥ*)—smiting the armies of the enemy
- दासीः (*dāsīḥ*)—those who cause obstruction to rites
- विश्वा विशः (*viśvā viśaḥ*)—all the hostile people
- आराय (*ārāya*)—for the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice

O Indra, with the help of these praises recited by us, smiting the armies of the enemy and protecting our armies without harming them, destroy the wrath of the enemy. With the help of these very praises, destroy for the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice all the hostile people who confront us, who are spread everywhere, and who obstruct the rites.
(Induced) by these (praises), protecting our assailing host, baffle, Indra, the wrath of the enemy : (induced) by them, overthrow, on the part of the Arya, all the servile races everywhere abiding.

O Indra, those enemies who are near, like kinsmen, and those who stand in a distant place, who coming towards us, harming us, are prepared for battle: make the strengths of both kinds of these enemies weak, deprived of force; the word "make" is to be supplied. Likewise destroy their prowess. Further, make the enemies of both kinds turn away, turn their faces from us.
- विधुरा (*vidhurā*)—so that they are in vain
- पराचः (*parācaḥ*)—so that all of them turn away

O Indra, whether they are our kinsmen or not, those enemies of ours who confront us, harm us and are ready for battle, make the strengths of such two groups be in vain. Destroy all their prowess. Make all of them turn away.
Annihilate, Indra, the strength of those who, whether kinsmen or unrelated, present themselves before us, exerting themselves as adversaries: enfeeble their prowess, put them to flight.

O Indra, the hero favoured by you slays with his limbs a hero, an enemy hero, as well; the particle वा (*vā*) here has the sense of "also". Or else, by this particle that expresses an alternative: even one who is not a hero, if favoured by you, slays a hero. When does he slay? When two rivals, shining with bodily splendour, wage battle in the fight; and whenever, for the sake of a son, or of cattle, or of a grandson, or of waters, or of fertile lands rich in every crop, the two cry out and dispute. The meaning is: O Indra, victory and the gain of sons and the like belong to one who is favoured by you.
- तनूरुचा (*tanūrucā*)—O Indra, the two opposing groups shining with the excellence of their bodies
- तोके वा (*toke vā*)—whether for the sake of a son
- गोपु (*gopu*)—or for the sake of cattle
- तनये (*tanaye*)—or for the sake of a grandson
- अप्पु (*appu*)—or for the sake of water
- उर्वरासु (*urvarāsu*)—or for the sake of land rich in crops
- वि ब्रवैते (*vi bravaite*)—they carry on harsh speech (in such circumstances)
- शरीरैः (*śarīraiḥ*)—by the powers of his limbs
- शूरं वा (*śūraṃ vā*)—even if his enemy is a hero, him

O Indra, when two opposing groups shining with the excellence of their bodies fight in battle, when for the sake of a son, or of cattle, or of a grandson, or of water, or of land rich in crops, they carry on harsh speech with the clamour of anger, in such circumstances the hero favoured by you destroys, by the strength of his own body, his enemy, even if that enemy is a hero.

The hero, (favoured by you), assuredly slays the (hostile) hero by his bodily prowess, when, both excelling in personal strength, they strive together in conflict, or when, clamorous, they dispute for (the sake of) sons, of grandsons, of cattle, of water, of land.

O Indra, no hero, no valiant man, does fight with you; he does not fight. Likewise one who is a destroyer of other enemies does not fight with you; and the assailant, the one who attacks, also does not fight with you.

The fighter who is enraged in battle, the warrior, does not fight with you. O Indra, among these heroes and the rest no one is a counterpart to you; you have no equal. All those heroes and the rest that have come into being, you overcome; you surpass them.
- धृष्णुः (*dhṛṣṇuḥ*)—even one who has the strength to confront others
- नकिः प्रत्यस्ति (*nakiḥ pratyasti*)—there is no hero who is equal

O Indra, no valiant man can fight with you; no swift-moving enemy can withstand you. Even one who has the strength to confront all others cannot withstand you. No warrior filled with self-esteem can fight with you. O Indra, among these heroes there is no hero who is equal to you; you are the lord of all things of prowess that have arisen in the world.

But you (no one) resists, neither the hero, nor the fleet runner nor the resolute, nor the combatant confiding (in his valour); neither of these, Indra. is a match for you : you are superior to all these persons.

Of these two parties, that man rules over nṛmṇa, wealth. The two things to be said are: between which two, and which of them rules. The particle यदि (*yadi*) stands in the sense of "of whom": he in whose sacrifice the priests, the performers of rites, call upon, that is, praise Indra, he is the one who rules; this is the connection. Whether it be in a great, abundant Vṛtra, that is, in an obstruction or on account of it, or in a dwelling attended by servants, that is, on account of a house, the two men who are व्यचस्वंतौ (*vyacasvaṃtau*) fight against each other; between those two, the connection is, that man rules.
- नृवति (*nṛvati*)—whether on account of servants and the like
- क्षये वा (*kṣaye vā*)—or on account of a house
- व्यचस्वंता (*vyacasvaṃtā*)—with the rivalry of each wishing to defeat the other
- अयोः उभयोः (*ayoḥ ubhayoḥ*)—among these two groups

In a great battle, whether on account of servants and the like or on account of a house, of the two opposing groups who fight with the rivalry of each wishing to defeat the other, he alone among these two groups obtains wealth for whom, as sacrificer, the priests praise Indra in the sacrifice.

Of both these (disputants), that one acquires wealth whose priests invoke (Indra) at the sacrifice, whether they contend emulous for (the overthrow of) a powerful enemy, or for a dwelling peopled with dependants.

And further, O Indra, whenever your people tremble with fear, be their protector, their guardian. And be also their वरूता (*varūtā*), that is, their sharer. O Indra, those of our men who are the best leaders and who bring you here, be their protector. O Indra, those praisers who have set us in front, be the protector of them too. ⟨NOTE:393⟩
notes: ಆ. ೨-೫: the bhāṣya gives the same sūtra as ಆ. ೯-೫

en: - वरूता (*varūtā*)—be to them a giver of refuge
- पुरः दधिरे (*puraḥ dadhire*)—have made foremost in the sacrifice (protect them also)

O Indra, when men who worship you tremble, remove their fear and protect them. Be a giver of refuge to them. Among men of excellent understanding such as we, protect also those who draw near to you. O Indra, protect also those praisers who have made us foremost in the sacrifice.

Therefore, Indra, when your people tremble (with fear), protect them; be to them a defender: may those who are our chief leaders be enjoyers (of your favour), as well as those (your) worshippers who have placed us foremost (to perform the sacrifice).

In the Sākamedha sacrifices, in the Māhendra iṣṭi, this verse is the yājyā of Indra Vṛtraghna. It is also given in the Sūtra: अनु ते दायि मह इंद्रियाय विश्वकर्मन्हविषा वावृधानः (*anu te dāyi maha iṃdriyāya viśvakarmanhaviṣā vāvṛdhānaḥ*), Ā. 2-18. In the ekāha called Anukrī ⟨NOTE:394⟩, in the niṣkevalya, it is the opening verse of the sūkta. It is also given in the Sūtra: अनु ते दायि मह इंद्रियाय कथो नु ते परि चराणि विद्वानिति द्वे (*anu te dāyi maha iṃdriyāya katho nu te pari carāṇi vidvāniti dve*), Ā. 9-5. O Indra, to you, the great one, for lordship all has been given in succession. On the occasion of the slaying of Vṛtra, all, in truth, has been given to you in succession. The two things given, and what they are, he states: the kṣatra, the strength by which he supports the universe, has been given; the sahas, the strength by which he overcomes enemies, qualified by that quality, has been given. O adorable Indra, in battle all this has been given to you by all the gods.
notes: ಭರದ್ವಾಜಸ್ತಾಂ ಚಷ್ಟೇ: ತಾಂ printed, the Kannada gloss has ತ್ವಾಂ

en: - अनु दायि (*anu dāyi*)—have been offered in order
- वृत्रहत्ये (*vṛtrahatye*)—for the destruction of the enemy
- क्षत्रं (*kṣatraṃ*)—the power that protects the world also
- सहः (*sahaḥ*)—the strength that destroys enemies also
- अनु (*anu*)—has been offered to you alone
- अनु (*anu*)—(all these riches) have been given

O Indra, of great form, all riches have been offered to you. For the destruction of the enemy, all that is of the nature of truth has been offered to you alone. The power that protects the world and the strength that destroys enemies have been offered to you alone. O worshipful Indra, all these riches have been given to you by the gods in battle.

All (power) has been successively conceded verily to you, Indra, who are mighty, for the destruction of the foe: suitable vigour, suitable strength in battle (has been given) to you, adorable Indra, by the goods.

In the Sākamedha sacrifices, in the iṣṭi performed to the deity Māhendra, in the oblation made to Indra Vṛtraghna, this Ṛk अनु ते दायि (*anu te dāyi*) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra, as explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra अनु ते दायि मह इंद्रियाय विश्वकर्मन् हविषा वावृधानः (*anu te dāyi maha iṃdriyāya viśvakarman haviṣā vāvṛdhānaḥ*) (Ā. 2-18). And in the ekāha sacrifice called Anukrī, at the beginning of the niṣkevalya śastra-mantras, this Ṛk is to be recited as the opening mantra of the sūkta, as explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra अनु ते दायि मह इंद्रियाय कथो नु ते परि चराणि विद्वानिति द्वे (*anu te dāyi maha iṃdriyāya katho nu te pari carāṇi vidvāniti dve*) (Ā. 2-5). ⟨NOTE:395⟩
notes: printed English of Ṛk 2 is followed by the word "unreadable" in the supplied text

en: O Indra, thus praised, in the battles drive on our armies, our hosts against the enemy, for the slaying of the enemy. And further, subdue for us the harming, godless, demonic armies; make them obedient for our sake. And, O Indra, we Bharadvājas, praising you, with food may surely obtain dwelling, that is, a home.
- भरद्वाजाः (*bharadvājāḥ*)—we who belong to the family of Bharadvāja

O Indra, thus praised, urge on in the battles our armies that fight with our enemies. Destroy the enemy armies that harm us, or make them submit to us. O Indra, may we, who praise you and belong to the family of Bharadvāja, surely obtain dwelling places endowed with wealth of food.

So (glorified by us), Indra, animate us (to overcome) our enemies in battle : overthrow our impious, malevolent (foes), and may we Bharadwajas, praising you, assuredly possess habitations, with (abundant) food.
O Indra, we, the praisers, sprinkling you with Soma, call upon you for the gain of great food, that is, of food in abundance.

You, Indra, hear that call of ours (श्रुधि (*śrudhi*) means "listen"). When, on a later day, in battle, the people assemble together, then grant us fierce protection, that is, protection that is raised aloft; "grant" is the sense of दाः (*dāḥ*) (अदाः (*adāḥ*)), "bestow".
- पारे अहन् (*pāre ahan*)—on the days ahead
- सं आयंत (*saṃ āyaṃta*)—will assemble together, then

O Indra, we who offer Soma call upon you, praying, for the gain of great food. Hear our praise. When, on the days ahead, men assemble together in battle, then grant us exceedingly great power and protection.
Hear us, Indra, when, offering libations, we call upon you for obtaining abundant food : grant us decided protection when on a future day men are assembling for battle.

वाजी (*vājī*) is one who has food in the form of oblations; वाजिनेयः (*vājineyaḥ*) is the son of Vājinī, Bharadvāja. O Indra, he invokes, that is, praises, you for the gain (सातौ (*sātau*)) of great food, food that is to be obtained by all (गध्यस्य (*gadhyasya*)). Moreover, O Indra, you are the protector of the good and the deliverer of the wicked; Bharadvāja calls upon you in the वृत्रेषु (*vṛtreṣu*), that is, in troubles and occasions of need. मुष्टिहा (*muṣṭihā*) is one who slays enemies by the strength of his fist; he who fights with enemies on account of cattle, Bharadvāja, looks upon you, that is, guards you. ⟨NOTE:396⟩
notes: ಯುದ್ಧಾದಹೀಪಲಃ: unclear word in the supplied text

en: - वाजी (*vājī*)—possessed of food in the form of oblation
- वाजिनेयः (*vājineyaḥ*)—Bharadvāja, the son of one called Vājinī
- वृत्रेषु (*vṛtreṣu*)—in the battle that destroys enemies
- मुष्टिहा (*muṣṭihā*)—one who kills the enemy with blows of the fist
- गोषु युध्यन् (*goṣu yudhyan*)—one who fights for the sake of cows, Bharadvāja

O Indra, Bharadvāja, who is possessed of food in the form of oblation and is the son of one called Vājinī, praises you for the gain of food that is desired by all and is great. O Indra, you are the protector of the good and the one who overcomes the wicked; Bharadvāja, who kills the enemy with blows of the fist in the battle that destroys enemies and who fights for the sake of cows, keeps looking to you.

The son of Vajini, (Bharadwaja), offering (sacrificial) viands, invokes you for (the sake of) acquiring obtainable and abundant food : (he invokes) you, Indra, the preserver of the good, the defender (from the wicked), when enemies (assail him): he depends upon you when, lifting up his fist, he is fighting for (his) cattle. ⟨NOTE:397⟩
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ. printed

en: O Indra, for the gain of food (अर्कसात् (*arkasāt*)) you urged on, that is, impelled, the sage Kavi, the Bhārgava seer. Moreover, O Indra, for Kutsa, who gave oblations, you cut down the asura Śuṣṇa (वर्क् (*vark*) means "you cut"). Likewise, wishing to bring about praiseworthy happiness for Atithigva, that is, for Divodāsa who goes to meet guests, you struck off the head of Śambara, who thought himself without a vital spot (अमर्मणः (*amarmaṇaḥ*)).
- अर्कसात् (*arkasāt*)—in the battle that is for the gain of food
- अमर्मणः (*amarmaṇaḥ*)—of the asura Śambara, possessed of the conceit that he is invulnerable

O Indra, in the battle that is for the gain of food you urged on the Bhārgava seer. For Kutsa, who offered oblation, you cut down the asura named Śuṣṇa. Wishing to bring about praiseworthy happiness for Divodāsa, who honours guests, you cut off the head of the asura Śambara, who was possessed of the arrogant conceit that he is invulnerable.

You have animated the sage with (the hope of) obtaining food : you have cut to pieces Sushna for Kutsa, the donor of the oblation : you have struck off the head (of Sambara), imagining himself invulnerable, intending to give pleasure to Atithigvan.
Kutsa is explained on pp. 694–696 of this same part; Śuṣṇa on pp. 636 and 724; Divodāsa in Part 9, p. 467; Śambara on p. 687 of this part and in Part 5, p. 694; Part 8, p. 274; Part 10, p. 550.

O Indra, you brought (प्र भरः (*pra bharaḥ*), "you caused to reach") to the king called Vṛṣabha a great chariot, the means of battle (योधं (*yodhaṃ*)). Moreover, you protected the king named Vṛṣabha, who was fighting with enemies and for whom ten days of fighting had passed (दशद्युं (*daśadyuṃ*)). ⟨NOTE:398⟩ Further, you, being a helper to the king called Vetasu, slew the asura Tugra. Vetasu is the name of a certain asura; here the one spoken of is another than he. Or else, वेतसवे (*vetasave*) is a dative used in the sense of the instrumental: you slew Tugra together with the asura Vetasu. And so it is heard in another mantra:

The mantra is quoted: अहं पितेव वेतसूरभिष्टये तुग्रं कुत्साय स्मदिभं च रंधयं । (*ahaṃ piteva vetasūrabhiṣṭaye tugraṃ kutsāya smadibhaṃ ca raṃdhayaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-49-4) **GLOSS** ⟨NOTE:399⟩. O Indra, you made Tuja, the king of that name, who praises you, to grow (तूतोः (*tūtoḥ*) means "you made grow").
notes: ಭಟಾನ್ದ್ರ ದರ್ಷಿ: stray ದ್ರ in the supplied text
ಯುಕ್ತಿ printed; ಋಕ್ಕು?

en: - योधं (*yodhaṃ*)—that which is the means of battle
- प्र भरः (*pra bharaḥ*)—provided, to the king named Vṛṣabha

O Indra, you provided to the king named Vṛṣabha a chariot that is the means of battle and is great. You protected that same Vṛṣabha, who fought for ten days. Being a helper to the king named Vetasu, you slew for him the asura named Tugra. O Indra, you made exalted the king named Tuja, who praises you.
You have brought to Vrishabha a great war-chariot; you have protected him warring for ten days: you have slain Tugra along with Vetasu: you have exalted Tuji glorifying you.

वृषभं (*vṛṣabhaṃ*)—if the bhāṣyakāra explains it as the king named Vṛṣabha, who is this king? What is his story cannot be made out. शंबरं (*śaṃbaraṃ*)—his story is explained on p. 687 and in 5-694, 8-274, 10-550. दिवोदासं (*divodāsaṃ*)—his story too is explained in Ṛ. Saṃ. Part 9, p. 467.

O Indra, you, the destroyer of enemies (बर्हणा (*barhaṇā*)), have done that praiseworthy deed. What is that deed? O hero, you have torn apart hundreds and thousands of Śambara's followers, his warriors. ⟨NOTE:400⟩ So in another Nigama: अध्वर्यवो यः शतं शंबरस्य । (*adhvaryavo yaḥ śataṃ śaṃbarasya |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-14-6) **GLOSS**. Likewise you slew the asura Śambara, the दासं (*dāsaṃ*), the destroyer of sacrifices and other rites, who had come out of the mountain. So it is also heard: यः शंबरं पर्वतेषु क्षियंतं । (*yaḥ śaṃbaraṃ parvateṣu kṣiyaṃtaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-12-11) **GLOSS**. Moreover, with manifold protections you protected, that is, cherished in an excellent manner, the king Divodāsa.
notes: abbreviation ಛಾಂ. ಉ. printed

en: - सहस्रा (*sahasrā*)—thousands in number, of Śambara's followers
- प्र दर्षि (*pra darṣi*)—you have torn apart
- गिरेः (*gireḥ*)—one who came out of the mountain

O Indra, you, the destroyer of enemies, have done many praiseworthy deeds. They are these: O valiant Indra, you have torn apart hundreds and thousands of Śambara's followers. You have slain the asura named Śambara, the destroyer of rites, who came out of the mountain. With protections of many kinds you have protected the king named Divodāsa.

Indra, you are the subduer (of foes), you have achieved a glorious (deed), inasmuch as you have scattered, hero, the hundreds and thousands (of the host of Sambara), have slain the slave Sambara (when issuing) from the mountain, and have protected Divodasa with marvellous protections.
शंबरं दिवोदासं (*śaṃbaraṃ divodāsaṃ*)—see the preceding Yukti. ⟨NOTE:401⟩
notes: ಸಿಷ್ಟಪ್ printed in the bhāṣya; the verse has ಸಿಸ್ವಪ್

en: O Indra, you are delighted (मंदसानः (*maṃdasānaḥ*) means "rejoicing") with deeds performed with faith, that is, with deeds carried out with great regard and in a spirit of faith. For a deed joined with faith becomes substantial; and so it is heard: यदेव विद्यया करोति श्रद्धयोपनिषदा तदेव वीर्यवत्तरं भवति । (*yadeva vidyayā karoti śraddhayopaniṣadā tadeva vīryavattaraṃ bhavati |*) (Chā. U. 1-1-10) **GLOSS** ⟨NOTE:402⟩. And delighted with Soma, you put to sleep, that is, slew, the asura Chumuri for the royal sage named Dabhīti. ⟨NOTE:403⟩ Moreover, O Indra, bestowing (दशस्यन् (*daśasyan*) means "giving") on Piṭhīnasa of that name the maiden called Raji, or else the kingdom, you by your wisdom (शच्या (*śacyā*)) slew at one and the same time sixty thousands, that is, sixty thousand warriors.
notes: English printed "ay we": initial M missing
abbreviations ಕೌ. ಬ್ರಾ., ಕಾ. ಸಂ., ಕೌ. ಉ. printed

en: - श्रद्धाभिः (*śraddhābhiḥ*)—by deeds done with faith, and
- दभीतये (*dabhītaye*)—for the royal sage called Dabhīti
- सिष्वप् (*siṣvap*)—you made to attain long sleep
- षष्टिं सहस्रा (*ṣaṣṭiṃ sahasrā*)—warriors numbering sixty thousand

O Indra, gratified by deeds done with faith and by Soma juices, you killed the asura called Chumuri for the royal sage called Dabhīti. Wishing to give the maiden called Raji to the one called Piṭhīnasa, you destroyed by your wisdom sixty thousand warriors at one time.

Delighted by libations offered with faith, you have consigned Chumuri to the sleep (of death) on behalf of Dabhiti, and bestowing (the maiden) Raji upon Pithinas, you have, by your contrivance, destroyed sixty thousand (warriors) at once.

Dabhīti: see p. 738 of this same part. Chumuri: see p. 687 of this same part. पिठीनसे रजिं (*piṭhīnase rajiṃ*)—since these names do not occur anywhere in the Ṛgveda other than in this Ṛk, nothing much can be known about them. The bhāṣyakāra has explained that Piṭhīnas is a man who was a friend of Indra, and that, in order to help them, he provided him with a maiden called Raja.

O सधवीर (*sadhavīra*), accompanied by heroes, O most powerful Indra: the heroes, that is, the praisers, praise the happiness and strength given by you, who are त्रिवरूथेन (*trivarūthena*), one for whom there are three enclosing worlds, and नहुषा (*nahuṣā*), the binder of enemies. That happiness and strength given by you, O Indra, which are exceedingly praiseworthy (ज्यायः (*jyāyaḥ*)), may I too, Bharadvāja, together with my praisers, obtain (आनश्यां (*ānaśyāṃ*) means "may I attain").
- सधवीर (*sadhavīra*)—one who is accompanied by heroes
- सूरिभिः (*sūribhiḥ*)—with the praisers who are with me

O Indra, accompanied by heroes and extremely mighty: the praisers praise the happiness and strength given by you, the protector of the three worlds and the binder of enemies. O Indra, that same praiseworthy happiness and strength given by you, may I and the other praisers who are with me obtain.

May I, with my fellow-worshippers, obtain that your most excellent felicity and vigour, which, most might Indra, associate of heroes, the pious celebrate (as bestowed) by you, who are the humiliator (of foes), the protector of the three (worlds).

O महिन (*mahina*), venerable Indra, may we, your friends, the praisers, be exceedingly dear to you in this praise, whose occasion is wealth (द्युम्नहूतौ (*dyumnahūtau*)). Prātardani is the son of a king named Pratardana; that son, Kṣatraśrī by name, my patron, a king, may be the best, that is, may be the most excellent of all. For what purpose? For the slaying of enemies (वृत्राणां (*vṛtrāṇāṃ*)) and for the acquiring of riches (धनानां (*dhanānāṃ*)), that is, of treasures. The connection is "may he be the best".
- अस्यां द्युम्नहूत् (*asyāṃ dyumnahūt*)—at this time of praise for the sake of wealth
- श्रेष्ठः अस्तु (*śreṣṭhaḥ astu*)—may he be more excellent than all

O venerable Indra, may we, your friends, be exceedingly dear to you in this time of praise that we perform for the sake of wealth. For the destruction of enemies and for the acquisition of riches, may the ruler called Kṣatraśrī, the son of Pratardana, be more excellent than all.

ay we, adorable Indra, your friends, at this your worship offered for (the acquirement of) wealth, be held most dear to you : may Kshatrashri, the son of Pratardana, (my patron), be most illustrious through the destruction of foes, and the attainment of riches. ⟨NOTE:404⟩
notes: ಆನಯೇಂದ್ರಮಾಕ್ಷಿಪತಿ: ಆನಯಾ read as part of the compound; unclear

en: प्रातर्दनिः क्षत्रश्रीः (*prātardaniḥ kṣatraśrīḥ*)—the son of Pratardana. It is stated in the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa (Kau. Brā. 25-5) that Pratardana was a descendant of Divodāsa. In the Kāṭhaka-saṃhitā (Kā. Saṃ. 21-10) there is a statement that the sage Bharadvāja was the priest of this king. In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (Kau. U. 3-1) there is mention of this king having met death in battle. Nothing much has come to be known about his son Kṣatraśrī. ⟨NOTE:405⟩
notes: ಮಘವನ್ಮನವನ್ನಿಂದ್ರ: ಮನವನ್ unclear

en: The seer Bharadvāja, impatient of delay in the reward, reproaches Indra. ⟨NOTE:406⟩ What did Indra do in the exhilaration of this Soma? And what did he do when this Soma was drunk, that is, at its drinking? What did he do in the friendship, the companionship, of this Soma? The sense is that before the drinking Indra dwells with Soma. And in the house (निषदि (*niṣadi*)) of this Soma, whatever praisers (रणा (*raṇā*)) there are: what did those praisers of former times obtain from you, O Indra? And what did the new, present-day praisers obtain?
notes: ದೀರ್ಘೋಽಭೂತ್ printed as the gloss of ದರ್ತ್; ದೀರ್ಣೋ?; also ವೃಜೀವತಃ and ವೃಚೀವಾನ್ spellings

en: - किं चकार (*kiṃ cakāra*)—what did he do
- कि मु (*ki mu*)—what did he do
- ये ना (*ye nā*)—among whatever praisers there are
- किं विविद्रे (*kiṃ vividre*)—what did they obtain
- नूतनासः (*nūtanāsaḥ*)—the praisers who are in the present time

As the result of the exhilaration obtained from this Soma juice, what reward did Indra give to the praisers? What did he do as the result of the drinking of this Soma? In the house of this Soma (the house of sacrifice), of whatever praisers there are who praise, what did the praisers who were before obtain from you? What have the praisers who are in the present time obtained?

What has Indra done in the exhilaration of this (Soma)? what has he done on quaffing this (libation)? what has he done in friendship for this (Soma)? what have former, what have recent adorers obtained from you in the chamber of this (libation)?
In this Ṛk the seer asks some questions on the matter of what benefits may be obtained from Indra's drinking of Soma, and has stated the answer to them in the next Ṛk.

Thus reproached, Indra gave the seer the wealth he desired. After that the seer, his wishes fulfilled by Indra, now refutes the statements conveying reproach which he had uttered before. Indra, in the exhilaration of this Soma, did a good (सत् (*sat*), that is, auspicious) deed; at the drinking of this Soma he did a good deed; in friendship with this Soma he did a good deed. Those who are praisers (रणा (*raṇā*)) in the house, that is, in the house of sacrifice: they, in former times, O Indra, obtained from you good deeds. The new, present-day praisers too obtain good deeds only.
- अस्य (*asya*)—by the drinking of this Soma juice
- अस्य (*asya*)—who is with the juice of this Soma
- नूतनासः (*nūtanāsaḥ*)—the praisers who are now present too
- स दु (*sa du*)—obtain a good result only

When Indra was satisfied by the drinking of Soma, he did good deeds. As the result of the drinking of this Soma he did good deeds only. Moreover, as the result of the friendship with this Soma juice also he did good deeds only. O Indra, all those praisers who were there in the house of sacrifice in the past obtained a good result only from you. The praisers who are present now also obtain a good result only.

Verily, in the exhilaration of this (Soma) Indra has done a good deed; on quaffing the libation (he has done) a good deed ; (he has done) a good deed in friendship for this Soma : former as well as recent adorers have obtained good of you in the chamber (of the libation).
O Maghavan, wealthy Indra, we do not know the greatness of all of you; we do not know it. ⟨NOTE:407⟩ Likewise, of your wealthiness
we do not know. Nor do we know all your wealth, your riches (राधसः (*rādhasaḥ*)), which is praiseworthy. O Indra, your capacity (इंद्रियं (*iṃdriyaṃ*)) is seen by no one.
notes: ಸೃಥೋರ್ವಂಶಜಸ್ಯ in the bhāṣya, ಪೃಥುವಂಶೋತ್ಪನ್ನ in the Kannada gloss

en: - मघवत्त्वस्य (*maghavattvasya*)—also the abundance of your wealth
- नकिः ददृशे (*nakiḥ dadṛśe*)—no one is able to see

O wealthy Indra, we do not know what your entire greatness is. We cannot know the abundance of your wealth. What your immeasurable riches are, we do not know. O Indra, it is not possible for anyone to comprehend your capacity.
We acknowledge no one, Maghavan, of greatness equal to you, nor one of like affluence, nor one of equally glorifiable riches, nor has (such as) your power been ever seen (in any other).

O Indra, by which prowess you slew the शेषः (*śeṣaḥ*) of Varaśikha (Varaśikha is the name of a certain asura), that is, his offspring, his sons (शेष (*śeṣa*) is a name for offspring): that prowess of yours, that very one, has been known by us (अचेति (*aceti*) means "has been known"). O Indra, by the sound alone of your thunderbolt hurled with that force, the Parama, a certain son excellent through superiority of strength among the sons of Varaśikha, was split asunder.
- ते यत् शुष्मात् (*te yat śuṣmāt*)—by which strength of yours
- स्वनात् चित् (*svanāt cit*)—by the sound alone
- परमः (*paramaḥ*)—Parama, the son of Varaśikha (the strongest of all of them)

O Indra, we know that capacity and power of yours by which prowess you slew all the sons of the asura named Varaśikha, and by which strength of yours, by the sound alone of the thunderbolt hurled, Parama, the son of Varaśikha, though the strongest of all of them, was split.

Such as your power (is) it has been comprehended (by us) as that wherewith you have slain the race of Varasikha, when the boldest (of them) was demolished by the noise of your thunderbolt hurled with (all your) force.

वरशिखस्य, परमः (*varaśikhasya, paramaḥ*)—Varaśikha was an asura king. The matter of his having been defeated by another king named Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna is stated in this Ṛk and in the next Ṛk. Parama is the son of Varaśikha.

By this Ṛk he explains the meaning stated before. This Indra, wishing to give the desired wealth (शिक्षन् (*śikṣan*)) to Abhyāvartin of that name, the son of King Cāyamāna, slew the शेषः (*śeṣaḥ*) of the asura Varaśikha, that is, his sons. How he slew the sons of Varaśikha is told: when this Indra at हरियूपीयायां (*hariyūpīyāyāṃ*) (Hariyūpīyā is the name of a certain river or a certain city), in its eastern half, that is, in its eastern part, slew the Vṛjīvat sons stationed there (Vṛcīvān is the name of an ancestor born in the family of Varaśikha; he slew the sons of Varaśikha born in his lineage), then the other, stationed in the western part, the best son of Varaśikha, was split through fear (भियसा (*bhiyasā*)). ⟨NOTE:408⟩
notes: ಜಾಯಮಾನಃ and ಜಯಮಾನ in the Kannada; the verse and the bhāṣya read ಚಾಯಮಾನಃ

en: - शिक्षन् (*śikṣan*)—wishing to give the desired wealth
- हरियूपीयायां (*hariyūpīyāyāṃ*)—of the river or city named Hariyūpīyā
- पूर्वे अर्थे (*pūrve arthe*)—on the bank of the eastern part
- वृजीवतः (*vṛjīvataḥ*)—all the sons of the Vṛjīvat lineage
- अपरः (*aparaḥ*)—another son of Varaśikha, who was on the other bank of the same river

Indra, wishing to give the desired wealth to the king named Abhyāvarti, the son of Cayamāna, slew the sons of the asura named Varaśikha. When he slew all the sons of the Vṛcīvat lineage who were on the bank of the eastern part of the river named Hariyūpīyā, then another son of Varaśikha, who was on the other bank of the same river, was split through fear alone (and died).

Favouring Abhyavartin, the son of Chayamana, Indra destroyed the race of Varasikha, killing the descendants of Vrichivat, (who were stationed) on the Hariyupiya, on the eastern part, whilst the western (troop) was scattered through fear.

हरियूपीयायां (*hariyūpīyāyāṃ*)—Hariyūpīyā is supposed to be the name of a river. This name occurs only in Ṛks 5 and 6 of this sūkta and nowhere else. It is stated that on the bank of this river the king named Abhyāvarti Cāyamāna fought a battle and destroyed the royal sons, or warriors, of the people called Vṛcīvantas.

Now he explains the meaning just stated. O Indra, called by many (पुरुहूत (*puruhūta*)), श्रवस्या (*śravasyā*) means "through desire for śravas", and śravas is food or fame. With the wish for that, in battle, having conquered you, we might obtain food.

Wishing "may we obtain fame", they came śarave, that is, to injure you. Advancing and approaching, breaking the vessels, the implements of the sacrifice, wearing armour, thirty hundred in number, that is, a hundred and thirty, the Vṛcīvants, sons of Varaśikha, together, at one and the same time, on the Yavyāvatī mentioned before, that is, the Hariyūpīyā, became "without purpose", devoid of meaning: they went, that is, they met destruction.
- पात्रा (*pātrā*)—the vessels that are the implements of the sacrifice
- त्रिंशच्छतं (*triṃśacchataṃ*)—a hundred and thirty in number
- यव्यावत्यां (*yavyāvatyāṃ*)—on the bank of the river Hariyūpīyā

O Indra, called by many, the sons of Varaśikha, who desired food, who gathered together to injure you, who destroyed the vessels that are the implements of the sacrifice, who wore battle armour and were a hundred and thirty in number, together on the bank of the river Hariyūpīyā, devoid of purpose, met destruction.

Indra, the invoked of many, thirty hundred mailed warriors (were collected) together on the Yavyavati, to acquire glory, but the Vrichivats advancing hostilely, and breaking the sacrificial vessels, went to (their own) annihilation.

Aruṣā means shining; suyavasya, desiring good grass; rerihāṇā, licking, tasting the fodder again and again; or else, making a special gait. The two horses of that Indra, which move between heaven and earth, in the atmosphere in the middle, go there. The words u and su are fillers. That Indra gave up Turvaśa the king to Sṛñjaya, a king of that name. Doing what? Subduing the Vṛcīvants, the sons of Varaśikha, for Daivavāta, that is, for the king Abhyāvartin, born in the line of Devavāta; or else, giving him their wealth.
- दैववाताय (*daivavātāya*)—to Abhyāvartin, born in the line of one called Devavāta

The Indra whose horses, golden-coloured, attractive, desiring the choicest grass, and leaping and running, move about between heaven and earth, subdued the sons of Varaśikha to Abhyāvartin, born in the line of Devavāta. He brought the enemy king called Turvaśa under the power of the king called Sṛñjaya.
He whose bright prancing horses, delighted with choice fodder, proceed between (heaven and earth), gave up Turvasa to Srinjaya, subjecting the Vrichivats to the descendant of Devavata, (Abhyavartin).

सृंजयाय (*sṛṃjayāya*)—a king of the people called Sṛñjaya. He was very famous. It can be understood from the description of the battle in this sūkta that the king Abhyāvarti Cāyamāna fought with Varaśikha and defeated him. This king Abhyāvarti is a descendant of one called Devavāta. There is no doubt at all that Sṛñjaya also belongs to this line. But Western scholars have expressed doubt whether these two are one and the same person. The Vṛcīvants mentioned in this sūkta may probably be Turvaśas themselves, or may be their friends. It is said in Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-15-4 that Sṛñjaya was the son of one called Devarāta. That Indra helped this Sṛñjaya and Abhyāvarti in battle is stated in this sūkta.

Now Bharadvāja declares to Agni the wealth given to him by Abhyāvartin. O Agni, the king, opulent, that is, wealthy and of abundant gifts, a sovereign, a performer of the Rājasūya, named Abhyāvartin, the son of Cāyamāna, gives me twenty cows, that is, animals, with chariots, with women, in pairs. Pārthavānām: it is related to Abhyāvartin, born in the line of Sṛthu; the plural is used for honour. ⟨NOTE:409⟩ This gift is durnaśā: no one can destroy it.
notes: ಆತ್ರೇಯಮನುಕ್ರಮಣಿಕಾ in the bhāṣya; abbreviation ಅ. ಗೃ. printed here, ಆ. ಗೃ. in the Kannada Anuvāda

en: - पार्थवानां (*pārthavānāṃ*)—of this Abhyāvarti, born in the line of Pṛthu
- इयं दक्षिणा (*iyaṃ dakṣiṇā*)—this gift in the form of a dakṣiṇā
notes: ಮೋದಯಥ in the gloss; the bhāṣya explains ಮೇದಯಥ as ಆಪ್ಯಾಯನಂ ಕುರುಥ

en: O Agni, the king called Abhyāvarti, wealthy, a sovereign, the son of Jayamāna, has given me animals with chariots, in the form of pairs, with women, twenty in number. The dakṣiṇā of this Abhyāvarti, born in the line of Pṛthu, cannot be destroyed by anyone.
The opulent supreme sovereign Abhyavartin, the son of Chayamana, presents, Agni, to me two damsels riding in cars, and twenty cows: this donation of the descendent of Prithu cannot be destroyed.

In this Ṛk it is explained that the king Abhyāvarti was born in the line of Pṛthu, and that he gave chariots, cows and the like to the seer Bharadvāja, the seer of this sūkta; the praise of that king's gift is also explained. In this Ṛk the seer Bharadvāja has told Agni about this gift.

May the cows come to our house. And may they do what is auspicious, welcome and good. May they also sit in our cowshed, the place of the cows, and afterwards take delight among us. And may many cows of various colours, with offspring, many in number, yielding milk for Indra at the times of dawn, be here in this cowshed.
- आ अग्मन् (*ā agman*)—may they come to our house
- सीदंतु (*sīdaṃtu*)—may they come and lie down
- रणयंतु (*raṇayaṃtu*)—may they be affectionate, may they be delightful

May the cows come to us and fill our place. May they bring us welfare. May they come and lie down in our cowshed. May they show affection among us and make us happy. May the cows of various colours, with good calves and great in number, yield milk for the sake of Indra at the times of dawn.
May the cows come and bring good fortune: let them lie down in (our) stalls and be pleased with us: may the many-coloured cows here be prolific, and yield milk for Indra on many dawns.
In this Ṛk and in the following Ṛks the explanation of the meaning is very easy and clear, so that no special explanation is necessary.

Indra gives to the sacrificer, one given to sacrifice, and to the praiser who pleases him with hymns, the wealth they desire. Not only once does he give, but always: approaching, he always gives. He never takes away the own wealth of the sacrificer and of the praiser. Further, increasing again and again the wealth he himself has given to either of these two, bringing it to growth, he places that person who longs for the god Indra in a khilya that cannot be broken by enemies; khila is a place that is not struck down, and khilya is the same. That is, he places him, he settles him, in a place that others cannot attack.
- शिक्षति (*śikṣati*)—gives the wealth that is desired
- न मुषायति (*na muṣāyati*)—does not take away again
- वर्धयन् इत् (*vardhayan it*)—causing it to grow
- अभिन्ने (*abhinne*)—that cannot be broken by enemies

Indra gives the wealth that is desired to the sacrificer who performs sacrifice and praises. He himself approaches him and gives. He does not take away again the wealth he has given. Causing the wealth of this sacrificer to grow again and again, he keeps him, the worshipper of the gods, placed in a protected region that enemies cannot enter.

Indra grants the desires of the man who offers to him sacrifice and praise; he ever bestows upon him wealth, and deprives him not of that which is his own: again and again increasing his riches, he places the devout man in an inaccessible fortress.

In the offerings to the divine ones, the two Ṛks beginning न ता नशंति (*na tā naśaṃti*) and the following are the yājyā and puronuvākyā of the cow deity, Ā. Sū. 6-14. In the Gostoma also these two stand at the opening of the sūkta in the Marutvatīya and Niṣkevalya. It is also laid down in the sūtra: न ता आर्वा रेणुककाटो अश्नुते न ता नशंति न दभाति तस्करः । (*na tā ārvā reṇukakāṭo aśnute na tā naśaṃti na dabhāti taskaraḥ |*), Ā. Sū. 9-5. Those cows do not perish: may they not be lost from us. Further, a thief, a robber, does not injure: may he not harm our cows. Likewise the weapon of the enemy, that which belongs to a foe, does not assault these cows: may it not attack. The master of such cows, the sacrificer, with the cows by which he performs sacrifice to the gods, Indra and the others, and which he gives for Indra, with such cows may he be united for a long time.
- न नशंति (*na naśaṃti*)—may they not be lost
- न दभाति (*na dabhāti*)—may he not steal
- आमित्रः (*āmitraḥ*)—that which belongs to an enemy
- न आ दधर्षति (*na ā dadharṣati*)—may it not attack
- गोपतिः (*gopatiḥ*)—the sacrificer, the master of these cows
- याभिः (*yābhiḥ*)—with the help of which cows
- देवांश्च (*devāṃśca*)—with Indra and the other deities in view
- ददाति च (*dadāti ca*)—and offers the oblation
- ताभिः सह (*tābhiḥ saha*)—together with those cows

May our cows not be lost. May the thief not steal them. May the weapon of an enemy not fall upon these cows. May the sacrificer, the master of these cows, remain united for a long time and be happy with those cows with whose help he performs sacrifice with Indra and the other deities in view and offers the oblation.

Let not the Cows be lost: let not thief carry them away: let no hostile weapon fall upon them: may the master of the cattle be long possessed of those with which he sacrifices, and which he presents to the gods.

It is explained in the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra (Ā. Sū. 6-14) that when the oblation called Daivī is offered, the two Ṛks न ता नशंति (*na tā naśaṃti*) (the third Ṛk) and न ता अर्वा (*na tā arvā*) (the fourth Ṛk) are to be recited as the yājyā and puronuvākyā mantras of the cow deity. And in the Gostoma also, at the beginning of the Marutvatīya and Niṣkevalya śastra mantras, these Ṛks are to be recited as the opening Ṛks of the sūkta; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra न ता अर्वा रेणुककाटो अश्नुते न ता नशंति न दभाति तस्करः (*na tā arvā reṇukakāṭo aśnute na tā naśaṃti na dabhāti taskaraḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 9-5).

Reṇukakāṭaḥ is one who breaks up the dust, the terrestrial dust; the root kaṭi has the sense of splitting. The horse that has come for battle does not reach those cows: may it not get at them. Likewise may those cows not go to the rite of slaughter and the like: may they not approach it. Further, may those cows roam about in particular, in the wide-ranging, fearless region of the sacrificer, that mortal man given to sacrifice.
- न अश्नुते (*na aśnute*)—may it not confront them and rush upon them
- संस्कृतत्रं (*saṃskṛtatraṃ*)—the rite of slaughter and the like, the state of being a sacrificial animal
- न अभ्युपयंति (*na abhyupayaṃti*)—may they not undergo
- यज्वनः (*yajvanaḥ*)—of the man who performs sacrifice
- तस्य मर्तस्य (*tasya martasya*)—of that mortal man
- वि चरंति (*vi caraṃti*)—may they roam freely

May the stout horse that raises the dust not confront those cows of ours and fall upon them. May those same cows, though they are animals in a sacrifice, not undergo that cutting up. And may they roam freely in the regions of the sacrificer that are fit for wide roaming and free from fear.
Let not the dust-spurning (war)-horse reach them; nor let them fall in the way of sacrificial consecration : let the cattle of the man who offers sacrifice wander about at large and without fear.

May the cows themselves be bhaga, wealth, for me. And may Indra give me cows. May the cows be the bhakṣa, the food, of the first, the best of the oblations, of Soma; for the pressed Soma is joined with the products of the cow, ghee and the like. O people, these cows that exist are those very ones, and those cows are Indra, because as curds, ghee and the like they nourish Indra. Such an Indra I desire with the heart, with a mind full of faith; the word cit has the sense of "also". Icchāmit means: I do desire. The meaning is: I wish to sacrifice to such an Indra with the cows as the means.
- प्रथमस्य (*prathamasya*)—of that which is offered first
- या गावः (*yā gāvaḥ*)—the cows that there are
- स इंद्र (*sa iṃdra*)—they are the very forms of that Indra
- हृदा (*hṛdā*)—with a mind full of faith

The cows are wealth to me. May Indra give me cows. May the cows provide milk and the like for the Soma that is offered first. O men, the cows that there are of this kind are the very forms of that Indra. Such an Indra I certainly desire with a mind full of faith.
May the Cows be (for our) affluence : may Indra grant me cattle : may the cows yeild the food of the first libation : these Cows, oh men. are Indra, the Indra whom I desire with heart and mind.

O cows, you medayatha, that is, you cause nourishment, you make plump. Likewise, even one that is emaciated, that is, wasted, and even one that is unlovely, inauspicious, you make suprātīka, beautiful of limb. O cows bhadravācaḥ, endowed with auspicious sound, make our house bhadra, auspicious: make it provided with cows. In the assemblies, the gatherings at the sacrifice, O cows, your great vayas, your abundant food, is spoken of: the meaning is that it is given by all.
- कृशं चित् (*kṛśaṃ cit*)—even if it is wasted
- अश्रीरं चित् (*aśrīraṃ cit*)—even if it is unlovely
- सुप्रतीकं कृणुथ (*supratīkaṃ kṛṇutha*)—make such limbs of ours shapely
- भद्रवाचः (*bhadravācaḥ*)—O cows, whose sounds are auspicious
- सभासु (*sabhāsu*)—in the assemblies of the sacrifice

O cows, cause us joy. Even if our limbs are wasted and unlovely, make such limbs of ours shapely. O cows, whose sounds are auspicious, make our house prosperous. Abundant food is offered to you in the assemblies of the sacrifice.

Do you, Cows, give us nourishment : render the emaciated, the unlovely body the reverse : do you, whose lowing is the auspicious, make my dwelling prosperous : great is the abundance that is attributed to you in religious assemblies.

O cows, be prajāvatīḥ, accompanied by calves; the verb "be" is understood. Be grazing on good grass, devouring it for food. Be also drinking pure, clean waters at a place easily drunk from, a pond or the like. May a thief, a robber, not become master over you. Likewise may a beast of prey, a tiger or the like, an enemy, not rule over you. Further, may the weapon of Rudra, the Supreme Lord, who is of the nature of time, turn away from you, avoid you.
- प्रजावतीः (*prajāvatīḥ*)—O cows, be accompanied by calves
- सुप्रपाणे (*suprapāṇe*)—in a pond fit for drinking at ease
- मा ईशत (*mā īśata*)—may he not become master
- अघशंसः (*aghaśaṃsaḥ*)—tigers and the like that cause you harm
- परि वृज्याः (*pari vṛjyāḥ*)—may it not encompass you, may it not fall upon you

O cows, be accompanied by your calves. Go on grazing the choicest grass. Go on drinking clean waters in a pond fit for drinking at ease. May a thief not become your master. May tigers and the like that cause you harm not injure you. May the weapon of Rudra not fall upon you.

May you, Cows, have many calves grazing upon food pasture, and drinking pure water at accessible ponds : may no thief be your master : no beast of prey (assail you), and may the (fatal) weapon of Rudra avoid you.

In these cows may this upaparcana, this nourishment, be joined. O Indra, in your vīrya, by reason of your potency, in the semen of the bull who places the embryo in the cows, there is this upaparcana, this nourishment. For when the cows are nourished, Indra is nourished through the oblations of milk and the like connected with them: this is the meaning. The repetition of upa is to fill out the pādas.
- इदं उपपर्चनं (*idaṃ upaparcanaṃ*)—this kind of nourishment
- उप पृच्यतां (*upa pṛcyatāṃ*)—let it be prayed for
- रेतसि (*retasi*)—in the semen let there be virility
Let it be prayed that the nourishment spoken of above be in these cows. O Indra, for the increase of your power, let there be virility in the semen of the bull.
Let the nourishment of Cows be solicited, let the vigour of the bull (be requsted), Indra, for your invigoration.

Since there is nourishment in the cattle, that is, in the cows, they yield milk in abundance. From milk, curds, ghee and the like come about, and the ghee (ājya) used in sacrifices and the like is obtained. By offering oblations with ājya and the like to Indra and the other deities, those deities are satisfied. For this reason it is prayed that there be nourishment in the cows. And since cows yield milk for some time only after they have calved, the matter that there be virility in the bull for the sake of calving is also stated here. For the increase of the progeny of cows it is necessary that there be virility in the semen of the bull. In the same way, for milk and the like to be obtained abundantly for the sacrifice, it is necessary that the cows calve and be well nourished. Therefore it is explained clearly in this Ṛk that both these works are very necessary, and that they come about only through the strength and power of Indra.
वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । पुमर्थांश्च तुरो देयाद्विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरः ॥ (*vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan | pumarthāṃśca turo deyādvidyātīrthamaheśvaraḥ ‖*) **GLOSS**

इति श्रीमद्राजाधिराज परमेश्वर वैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तक श्री वीरबुक्क भूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणाचार्येण विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये चतुर्थाष्टके षष्ठोऽध्यायः समाप्तः ॥ (*iti śrīmadrājādhirāja parameśvara vaidikamārgapravartaka śrī vīrabukka bhūpālasāmrājyadhuraṃdhareṇa sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye caturthāṣṭake ṣaṣṭho 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ ‖*) **GLOSS**
Here ends the sixth adhyāya, in the fourth aṣṭaka, of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, with the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and the Kannada translation.
यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव वागीश्वर नमोऽस्तुते ॥ (*yadakṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yadbhavet | tatsarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva vāgīśvara namo 'stute ‖*) **GLOSS**
